books.title: How Animals Sleep
books.art_why: Real animals and their sleeping habits can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction Almost all animals need to sleep to stay healthy. But sleeping can be dangerous. Other animals may hunt sleeping animals. Animals have many different ways of sleeping that help them stay safe. Some of these ways may surprise you!
pages.brief: A group of animals are asleep in a natural setting, with one animal resting while another watches nearby. The scene suggests that sleep is needed but can be dangerous, and that animals have many different ways of sleeping to stay safe.

pages.text: Sleeping Upside Down Almost all bats sleep upside down. They hang by their toes from a branch or from the ceiling of a cave. Up high, bats are safe from most other animals. If they are in danger, they just fly away.
pages.brief: Several bats hang upside down by their toes from a cave ceiling and from a branch, high above the ground. They are safe up there from most other animals, and one bat is ready to fly away if danger comes near.

pages.text: Sleeping the Most and the Least Little brown bats win the prize for sleeping the most. They sleep as much as nineteen hours a day. These bats are only awake for a few hours after the Sun goes down. They may get up again for a little while before the Sun rises. The rest of the time is for sleep, sleep, sleep!
pages.brief: Little brown bats hang asleep in a dark roost. They sleep for up to nineteen hours a day; a few are awake in the dim light after sunset, and the rest keep sleeping through the long hours.

pages.text: Giraffes win the prize for sleeping the least. They lie down when they sleep. They rest their heads on their bodies or on the ground. Every few hours, they sleep for about ten minutes. Giraffes are not safe if they sleep for long periods.
pages.brief: A giraffe lies down to sleep, resting its head on its body or on the ground. It sleeps for only about ten minutes every few hours, because a giraffe is not safe if it stays asleep for long periods.

pages.text: Sleeping with Half the Brain A dolphin sleeps with just half its brain at a time. It must stay awake to breathe and to watch for danger. Dolphin mothers and babies can go without sleep for as long as two months to stay safe.
pages.brief: A dolphin floats near the surface of the sea, resting half its brain while staying awake to breathe and watch for danger. A dolphin mother and her baby swim close together, able to go without sleep for as long as two months.

pages.text: Some ducks sleep with just half their brains, too. These ducks often sleep in a line. The ducks at both ends help keep the group safe. They keep one eye open to watch for danger. The ducks in the middle sleep deeply with both eyes closed.
pages.brief: A row of ducks sleeps in a line, with the ducks at both ends keeping one eye open to watch for danger. The ducks in the middle sleep deeply with both eyes closed, helping the group stay safe.

pages.text: Sleeping Underwater Seals breathe air, but that doesn’t stop some of them from sleeping underwater. They hold their breath and dive deep to sleep for up to twenty minutes at a time. Sleeping deep underwater helps these seals stay safe from animals that hunt them near the surface.
pages.brief: A seal dives deep underwater and holds its breath as it sleeps for up to twenty minutes at a time. Far below the surface, it is safer from animals that hunt near the top of the water.

pages.text: Some fish make their own sleeping bags. They make a big spit bubble and sleep inside it. The bubble keeps them in one place all night. It also keeps other animals from smelling them. If an animal bumps the bubble, the fish swims away.
pages.brief: A fish rests inside a large spit bubble it has made around itself underwater. The bubble keeps the fish in one place all night and hides its smell from other animals; if an animal bumps the bubble, the fish swims away.

pages.text: Sleeping Standing Up Horses often sleep standing up. Their legs lock in place so they don’t fall over. If a horse is lying down, it needs a long time to get up. A horse can run from danger more quickly if it is already standing.
pages.brief: A horse stands asleep with its legs locked in place so it will not fall over. It is already on its feet, ready to run from danger more quickly than a horse that has been lying down and needs a long time to get up.

pages.text: A flamingo can sleep while standing on one leg. The standing leg locks so it stays straight. The other leg tucks up close to the flamingo’s body. Its head rests on its back. A flamingo lives (and sleeps) near many other birds to stay safe.
pages.brief: A flamingo sleeps while standing on one leg. Its standing leg is locked straight, the other leg is tucked close to its body, and its head rests on its back. Many other birds stand nearby in the same place.

pages.text: Sleeping While Flying Some seabirds can sleep while they fly. These large birds spend most of their lives over the ocean. They are in danger on the water, but they are safe in the air. They glide for many hours without flapping their wings. Sometimes they sleep while they glide.
pages.brief: A large seabird glides over the ocean without flapping its wings, asleep in the air. Other seabirds glide nearby, spending most of their lives over the water, where they are in danger, but safe while they fly.

pages.text: Conclusion The animals on this page are sleeping, too. Would you like to sleep how they sleep?
pages.brief: Several animals rest asleep in different ways in one scene: some stand, some lie down, some hang, and some float. Each sleeps in a way that helps it stay safe, showing the many different sleeping habits of animals.

books.title: Oil: A Messy Resource
books.art_why: Real oil rigs, tankers, spills and shorelines exist today, so photographs show them accurately.

pages.text: Introduction Oil is a very important resource. We use oil for energy. We use it to make gas for cars. We use it to heat buildings. We even use it to make plastic things and medicines.
pages.brief: A gasoline pump fills a car at a station, a nearby building glows with heat, and a table holds plastic containers, toys and medicine bottles. These everyday things all come from oil, which is used for energy, fuel, heat, plastic and medicine.

pages.text: Oil comes from below the ground. We use large drills to dig wells. The wells bring oil to the surface. Then we can use the oil.
pages.brief: A large drill bores down through soil and rock to make a well. Dark oil rises up the well pipe toward the surface, where it can be collected and used. The ground is cut away so the deep well and the rising oil are visible.

pages.text: The oil derrick helps lift pipes that go in the well. 3 Pipes are used to help bring oil to the surface. The pipes keep the oil from getting in the water. 2 Oil is often found under layers of rock. The rock keeps the oil from rising to the surface on its own. How We Get Oil Oil is found in many places. Some of these places are below land, but others are below the ocean floor.
pages.brief: An oil derrick stands over a well, lifting long pipes. The pipes carry oil up from a deep pool trapped beneath layers of rock. Below the land and below the ocean floor, oil waits in the ground in many places around the world.

pages.text: An oil rig is a machine that drills for oil. Oil rigs drill deep into the ground. Some special oil rigs can float on the ocean. They use pipes to bring the oil to the surface.
pages.brief: An oil rig drills deep into the ground, its tall machinery working above the well. A special floating rig sits on the ocean, held above the water, with pipes reaching down to bring oil up from below the seafloor.

pages.text: Problems with Drilling Underwater Problems can happen when people drill for oil. This floating oil rig caught fire. Some people were killed, and others got hurt.
pages.brief: A floating oil rig burns on the ocean, flames and thick black smoke pouring from its deck. The damaged structure tilts above the water as the fire continues, showing how dangerous underwater drilling can be for the people working there.

pages.text: ALABAMA MISSISSIPPI FLORIDA Mobile LOUISIANA Deepwater Horizon Oil Spill KEY Booms Beached oil Wildlife reserves Deepwater Horizon oil rig Oil looks red floating on the ocean’s surface. The oil rig burned and sank into the water. Oil from the well below the rig began to leak into the ocean.
pages.brief: A map shows the Gulf Coast, where red oil floats on the ocean surface after the Deepwater Horizon rig burned and sank. The spilled oil spreads across the water near the coast, and the sunken rig sits below the waves.

pages.text: Off icials look for signs of oil on shore. When lots of oil leaks from a well, it makes an oil spill. Oil spills can become very large. Oil spills cause harm to people and other animals.
pages.brief: Officials in protective gear walk along a shore, searching for signs of oil washed up by the water. A large oil spill spreads offshore, and the oily mess can harm people and animals that live along the coast.

pages.text: When oil floats to the shore, it covers everything. Sand and rocks get covered. Birds and other animals get covered. Oil makes a mess and can kill many plants and animals.
pages.brief: Oil covers a sandy shore and dark rocks at the water's edge. A bird stands coated in thick oil, unable to clean itself. Plants and animals along the beach are trapped in the messy oil, which can kill many of them.

pages.text: Other Sources of Oil Spills Wells are not the only cause of oil spills. Oil tankers are big ships that carry oil across oceans. If an oil tanker crashes or sinks, lots of oil can get in the water. It can take years to clean up the mess from a large oil spill.
pages.brief: A huge oil tanker sails across the ocean carrying oil. In another view, the ship has crashed or sunk, and dark oil spreads across the water in a wide slick, a mess that can take years to clean up.

pages.text: What People Think About Oil Drilling Some people think we should not drill for oil under oceans. Some people think we should not ship oil in large tankers. They say it would be easy for something to go wrong. They say that oil spills could happen.
pages.brief: A group of people stand together on a beach, looking out at an offshore oil rig. They frown and talk, worried that drilling under the ocean or shipping oil in big tankers could easily go wrong and cause an oil spill.

pages.text: Other people think we should keep drilling for oil under oceans. These people think we can find safe ways to drill for oil and carry it on ships. They say that good rules help keep oil spills from happening.
pages.brief: Workers in hard hats stand on an oil rig, checking pipes and equipment. They talk with engineers who believe careful drilling and strong safety rules can keep oil spills from happening while oil is taken from under the ocean.

pages.text: Conclusion Everyone agrees that oil spills are bad. But it’s also true that oil is an important resource. Do you think drilling for oil under the ocean is a good idea? Do you think we can take a chance on another oil spill happening?
pages.brief: People of different ages stand on a clean beach, talking together with an offshore oil rig far out on the water. They discuss whether drilling under the ocean is a good idea and whether the risk of another oil spill is worth taking.

books.title: Bigger Than a Monster Truck
books.art_why: Modern vehicles are real and can be photographed today.

pages.text: Big Movers Have you ever seen a monster truck? Monster trucks are big! They aren’t the biggest vehicles, though. What’s even bigger than a monster truck?
pages.brief: A huge monster truck with oversized tires stands on flat ground, shown from a low angle so it looks tall and powerful. The truck is clearly big, but the open space around it leaves room to wonder what vehicle could be even bigger.

pages.text: Vehicles That Move Things and People The Duck The “Duck” is a truck that can travel on both land and water. On land, the Duck moves around on six wheels. In water, the Duck floats like a boat. The Duck can carry people to places that are hard to reach.
pages.brief: A boxy Duck truck with six wheels drives on land beside water. In another view, the same Duck floats like a boat, carrying people across the water to a place that is hard to reach.

pages.text: Vehicle Bridge This vehicle is a bridge that can move. Other vehicles can drive over the bridge. When the bridge is no longer needed, it folds up onto the vehicle.
pages.brief: A special vehicle carries a bridge on its back. Other vehicles drive over the bridge to cross a gap. When the bridge is no longer needed, the bridge folds up and rests on the vehicle again.

pages.text: Cranes Cranes lift and move heavy things. Some cranes help workers build tall buildings. Others are used to move goods from ships to land.
pages.brief: A tall crane lifts a heavy load while workers build a tall building. At a port, another crane moves goods from a ship onto land. The cranes use strong arms and cables to lift and move the heavy things.

pages.text: Dump Trucks The world’s biggest dump trucks are used at mines. Miners use these trucks to carry rocks and dirt. The trucks use some of the biggest tires in the world. Their tires are twice as tall as a person.
pages.brief: At a mine, a giant dump truck carries rocks and dirt. Miners work nearby. The truck’s enormous tires are twice as tall as a person, making the whole vehicle look massive against the rocky ground.

pages.text: Overland Trains These trains are used to move heavy things to places without roads. The trains move on big wheels instead of on train tracks. Each wheel is taller than a person.
pages.brief: An overland train moves heavy things across ground without roads. Instead of train tracks, it rolls on huge wheels. Each wheel is taller than a person, and the train carries its load over rough land.

pages.text: Moving Space Vehicles Some of the world’s biggest vehicles were made to move things that go into space. They carry space vehicles on a high platform. These vehicles are so wide that they need their own road.
pages.brief: A gigantic transporter carries a space vehicle on a high platform. The vehicle is extremely wide, so it travels on its own wide road. It moves the space vehicle slowly toward the place where it will go into space.

pages.text: Vehicles That Dig Giant Power Shovels Miners use giant power shovels to dig rocks and dirt out of a mine. Giant power shovels have a big bucket that can break into the earth and scoop it up.
pages.brief: At a mine, a giant power shovel digs rocks and dirt. Its big bucket breaks into the earth and scoops up the loose material. Miners stand nearby as the huge machine works at the mine.

pages.text: Tunnel Diggers These vehicles dig under the surface of the earth. They can even move through solid rock.
pages.brief: A tunnel digger works under the surface of the earth. The huge machine moves through solid rock, leaving a tunnel behind it. Deep underground, it is surrounded by rock as it digs forward through the earth.

pages.text: The largest vehicle in the world is the Bagger 288. This huge vehicle digs mines. The Bagger 288 is almost as long as two football fields. Do You Know? People have built enormous vehicles since ancient times. The Helepolis (heh–LEH-puh-lis) was a huge tower built on wheels. It was used in battles in ancient Greece. The Helepolis was so heavy that more than three thousand people were needed to move it.
pages.brief: A gigantic Bagger 288 mining vehicle stretches across a mine, almost as long as two football fields. In a separate scene, an ancient Greek Helepolis tower on wheels is used in battle, with more than three thousand people needed to move the heavy tower.

pages.text: It digs with a huge wheel. The wheel has buckets along its edge that scoop up dirt as the wheel turns. The Bagger 288 is big enough to move mountains.
pages.brief: A close view shows the Bagger 288 digging with a huge wheel. Buckets along the wheel’s edge scoop up dirt as the wheel turns. The giant machine is big enough to move mountains of earth at the mine.

pages.text: Big Vehicles Big vehicles are used in many ways. These vehicles move heavy loads. They travel both above and below the ground. Gigantic vehicles have gotten much bigger over the years. Some of these vehicles keep getting bigger and bigger. How big are they going to get?
pages.brief: Several huge vehicles are shown moving heavy loads in different places. One big vehicle travels above ground, while another works below ground. The gigantic machines look larger than earlier models, and some appear ready to keep getting bigger.

books.title: Plant Defenses
books.art_why: Real plants and animals that exist today are shown.

pages.text: Introduction Animals have many ways to defend themselves and stay safe. Some have sharp claws, teeth, or horns. Others change color or hide in a shell. Some animals simply run away from danger. Plants can’t bite, fight, or run away. However, they have many other ways to protect themselves.
pages.brief: A group of animals shows defenses: one with sharp claws, one with teeth, one with horns, one tucked in a shell, and one running away. Nearby, several plants stand rooted in the ground, unable to bite, fight, or run.

pages.text: Thorns, Prickles, and Spines Some plants grow thorns on their branches. Animals that try to eat those plants can get cut or scratched. Some trees have long thorns that keep animals away.
pages.brief: A close view of a tree branch with long, sharp thorns. A browsing animal reaches toward the leaves and stops near the thorns, which can cut or scratch animals that try to eat the plant.

pages.text: Roses and some other plants have prickles on their stems. Prickles are different from thorns. Prickles grow out of a plant’s soft stem. Most often, prickles grow on small shrubs and flowering plants. Thorns usually grow on trees or large shrubs.
pages.brief: A rose stem with prickles growing out of its soft stem, beside a small flowering shrub. In the background, a tree branch shows thorns, making clear that prickles and thorns grow on different kinds of plants.

pages.text: Some plants have spines to defend themselves. Some plants are covered in spines to protect them from being eaten. Spines look and feel like thorns, but they are different.
pages.brief: A plant covered all over in sharp spines, shown close enough to see how they look and feel like thorns. The spines cover the plant's surface, defending it from animals that might try to eat it.

pages.text: Amazing Spines The hairy cactus, also known as the old man cactus, is covered with white hairlike strands. These strands protect it from sunlight, and help hide its sharp spines. A cactus spine is actually a special kind of leaf. Cactus plants usually live in hot deserts. Regular leaves may dry out in the hot sun, but sunlight and heat bounce off spines.
pages.brief: The hairy cactus, or old man cactus, stands in a hot desert. White hairlike strands cover it, protecting it from sunlight and hiding its sharp spines. Sunlight and heat bounce off the spines instead of drying out regular leaves.

pages.text: Stinging Plants Stinging plants have hairs that can poke animals that are trying to eat them. Inside each hair is a small tube with stinging fluid. The tip of this tube breaks easily.
pages.brief: A stinging plant with fine hairs on its leaves. A magnified view shows one hair as a small tube filled with stinging fluid, with a tip that breaks easily when an animal tries to eat the plant.

pages.text: When an animal bumps the hair, the tip breaks off and shoots fluid into the animal. Each leaf of a nettle plant has hundreds of stinging hairs.
pages.brief: A nettle leaf covered with hundreds of stinging hairs. An animal's skin bumps the hairs; one tip breaks off and shoots stinging fluid into the animal. The close view shows the nettle leaf and the broken hair.

pages.text: Poison Plants Some plants make poison to protect themselves. Eating one of these plants can cause an animal to get sick or even die. Deadly nightshade makes a powerful poison. This poison is found in all parts of the plant. Eating just one leaf can kill a large animal. peppermint Do You Know? Poisonous plants are not poisonous to every animal. The peppermint plant smells and tastes good to people, but it is harmful to insects.
pages.brief: Deadly nightshade grows with leaves full of powerful poison, and a large animal stands near it. Beside it, a peppermint plant has a person nearby enjoying its smell and taste, while insects nearby are harmed by it.

pages.text: Hidden Plants Some plants hide from animals by blending in with the ground where they grow. The living stone plant grows in dry, rocky ground among pebbles and stones. This plant looks like just another small stone. Animals do not see it as something to eat.
pages.brief: The living stone plant grows in dry, rocky ground among pebbles and stones. Its shape and surface look just like another small stone, so an animal nearby does not see it as something to eat.

pages.text: Other Defenses When an animal bumps a touch- me-not plant, the plant folds up its leaves. The thin, folded leaves do not look as tasty as full leaves. Also, a plant that moves may scare away an insect or other animal trying to eat it.
pages.brief: A touch-me-not plant with thin leaves. A small insect bumps the plant, and the leaves fold up. The folded leaves look less tasty than full leaves, and the plant's movement may scare away the insect or another animal.

pages.text: The tobacco plant plays a trick on the pests that eat it. When an insect bites a leaf, the plant sends out a special smell. This smell invites enemies, such as the big-eyed bug, to eat the invading insect.
pages.brief: An insect bites a tobacco plant leaf. The plant sends out a special smell, shown as wavy trails in the air. The smell invites enemies, such as the big-eyed bug, which approaches to eat the invading insect.

pages.text: Conclusion Plants might look defenseless at first, but they have powerful defenses to help them survive. Even without claws or horns like some animals, plants can protect themselves.
pages.brief: Several plants stand together in the ground, looking ordinary at first but healthy and strong. They have no claws or horns like some animals, yet their own powerful defenses help them survive where they grow.

books.title: Chichén Itzá
books.art_why: The book describes an ancient Maya city before photographs, so drawings fit the historical subject.

pages.text: A Building in the Jungle Long ago, ancestors of the Maya people built a city in the jungle. The city is named Chichén Itzá (chee-CHEN eet-SAH). The name means “at the mouth of the well of Itzá.” This city is an important place in the history of the Maya people.
pages.brief: Long ago in the jungle, ancestors of the Maya people build a city of stone. The city, Chichén Itzá, rises among dense green trees. Its name is linked to the well of Itzá. The scene shows the ancient city as an important place in Maya history.

pages.text: The Yucatán Chichén Itzá is on the Yucatán (yoo-kah-TAHN) Peninsula, in Mexico. There are a few big cities on the peninsula. The land around Chichén Itzá is mostly jungle, forest, and farms. Maya Lands Chichén Itzá GULF OF MEXICO BELIZE MEXICO GUATEMALA PACIFIC OCEAN HONDURAS EL SALVADOR.
pages.brief: The Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico is shown with a few big cities. Around Chichén Itzá, the land is mostly jungle, forest and farms. Nearby lands include Belize, Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador, with the Gulf of Mexico and Pacific Ocean.

pages.text: An Old City Chichén Itzá was built many hundreds of years ago by the Maya people. They made stone buildings that still stand today. The building at the center of the city is a tall stepped pyramid.
pages.brief: An old city stands with stone buildings built many hundreds of years ago by the Maya people. The buildings still stand today. At the center is a tall stepped pyramid. The scene shows the ancient city and its central pyramid.

pages.text: The Great Ball Court in Chichén Itzá is a big field with a stone wall. People played a game using a rubber ball. They moved the ball with their elbows, hips, and knees, but not their hands.
pages.brief: In the Great Ball Court, a big field has a stone wall. People play a game with a rubber ball. They move the ball with their elbows, hips and knees, not their hands. The court is in Chichén Itzá.

pages.text: Building Chichén Itzá It took many different Maya groups hundreds of years to build the city. The older buildings are low and flat. They often have plain stones on the bottom and fancy carved stones on top. Other buildings, like the stepped pyramid and the Great Ball Court, are different. They have animals carved on tall columns.
pages.brief: Maya groups build Chichén Itzá over hundreds of years. Older buildings are low and flat, with plain stones at the bottom and fancy carved stones on top. The stepped pyramid and the Great Ball Court have animals carved on tall columns.

pages.text: A Special Spot The Maya had an important reason to build a city where they did. This part of Mexico has no rivers or lakes. Instead, fresh water comes up from underground wells called cenotes (say-NOH-tayz). Chichén Itzá has two cenotes.
pages.brief: The Maya choose a special spot for their city. This part of Mexico has no rivers or lakes. Fresh water comes up from underground wells called cenotes. Chichén Itzá has two cenotes. The scene shows the dry land and the two cenotes.

pages.text: When many people moved away from the city, some people stayed behind. Having fresh water close by made it a good place to live.
pages.brief: Some people stay behind when many others move away from the city. Fresh water is close by, making the place good to live. The scene shows a few Maya people remaining near Chichén Itzá and its nearby water.

pages.text: The Maya got fresh water to drink from one of the cenotes. The other one was for gifts to Chac, the rain god. The Maya believed that if Chac liked the gifts, he would send rain. The rain would help their corn and other vegetables grow.
pages.brief: The Maya get fresh water to drink from one cenote. At the other cenote, they give gifts to Chac, the rain god. They believe Chac will send rain if he likes the gifts. Rain helps their corn and other vegetables grow.

pages.text: There are many important gods in Maya culture. Many buildings at Chichén Itzá are temples. The temples are places where people can give gifts to the gods. The stepped pyramid has a temple at the top for a god that looks like a snake with wings. This is the Maya god of creation.
pages.brief: Many important gods are in Maya culture. Many buildings at Chichén Itzá are temples where people give gifts to the gods. The stepped pyramid has a temple at the top for a god that looks like a snake with wings, the Maya god of creation.

pages.text: The Maya Today Many Maya people still live near their old cities. Maya people speak more than thirty languages. Their words for house, sun, time, mother, and corn sound alike in all Mayan languages. The Maya still watch the sky, which helps them know when to plant crops.
pages.brief: Many Maya people still live near their old cities. They speak more than thirty languages. Their words for house, sun, time, mother and corn sound alike in all Mayan languages. The Maya still watch the sky to know when to plant crops.

pages.text: Seeing Chichén Itzá Today More than one million people visit Chichén Itzá each year! Visitors used to climb the stepped pyramid if they wanted to. Over time, the steps broke down and became dangerous. The people of Mexico want to keep the building and visitors safe. Today, visitors are not allowed to climb the steps.
pages.brief: More than one million people visit Chichén Itzá each year. Visitors used to climb the stepped pyramid. Over time, the steps broke down and became dangerous. Mexico wants to keep the building and visitors safe. Today visitors are not allowed to climb the steps.

pages.text: A Wonderful Place Chichén Itzá was picked as one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. The city has amazing buildings that show the skill of the Maya people.
pages.brief: Chichén Itzá is picked as one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. The city has amazing buildings that show the skill of the Maya people. The scene shows the stepped pyramid and other stone buildings of Chichén Itzá standing together.

books.title: Big Ben and Westminster Palace
books.art_why: The book includes historical scenes such as the 1834 fire, old Westminster Hall and Pugin planning the clock, so drawings suit the past.

pages.text: An average-sized person could fit inside Big Ben many times over. A Famous Bell Big Ben is a huge bell at the top of a tall clock tower in London, England. The bell is as heavy as two elephants. Big Ben, the tower, and the clock are all important. They are part of Westminster Palace, which is home to Parliament. People all over the world have heard of Big Ben.
pages.brief: A huge bell hangs high in a tall clock tower in London. Beside it, an average-sized person stands to show how large the bell is, and two elephants suggest its great weight. The tower and clock rise above Westminster Palace, where Parliament meets.

pages.text: Parliament and Big Ben.
pages.brief: The view shows Parliament and Big Ben together. The huge bell is inside the tall clock tower, and the Parliament buildings stand beside it. The tower and the bell are the main subject in one scene.

pages.text: An Old Building Westminster Palace has several buildings. The oldest building is Westminster Hall. The hall is more than nine hundred years old and is still used today. Kings and queens lived at Westminster until 1512.
pages.brief: Westminster Hall stands as the oldest building in Westminster Palace. The great hall has stood for more than nine hundred years and is still used today. In the past, kings and queens lived at Westminster until 1512.

pages.text: Burned Down and Built Up A fire in 1834 burned most of Westminster Palace. Six years later, there was a search to find someone to build the palace again. Charles Barry got the job. It took thirty years and a lot of money to build the new palace.
pages.brief: A great fire in 1834 burns most of Westminster Palace. Six years later, people search for someone to build the palace again. Charles Barry gets the job. Building the new palace takes thirty years and a lot of money.

pages.text: Augustus Pugin planned the clock that is part of the tower. Pugin decided to make a clock with four faces—one on each side. Each clock face has 312 pieces of glass.
pages.brief: Augustus Pugin plans the clock for the tower. He decides to make a clock with four faces, one on each side. Each clock face is made with 312 pieces of glass. The clock is shown as part of the tall tower.

pages.text: Westminster Palace has three towers. For many years, the Victoria Tower was the largest square stone tower in the world. The Elizabeth Tower is the clock tower that holds Big Ben. The Central Tower was planned as a chimney for smoke from fireplaces inside the palace. Westminster Palace.
pages.brief: Westminster Palace has three towers. For many years, the Victoria Tower is the largest square stone tower in the world. The Elizabeth Tower is the clock tower that holds Big Ben. The Central Tower is planned as a chimney for smoke from fireplaces inside the palace.

pages.text: Parliament Westminster Palace is home to Parliament. Parliament is where people make laws for the United Kingdom. There are two houses in Parliament. People in the House of Commons help to decide what laws to make. They debate what the people need.
pages.brief: Parliament meets in Westminster Palace, where people make laws for the United Kingdom. Two houses sit in Parliament. In the House of Commons, people debate what the people need and help decide what laws to make.

pages.text: People in the House of Lords have titles, such as Lord and Lady. Others are important members of the Church of England. The House of Lords works with the House of Commons to make laws. When everyone agrees, the laws become Acts of Parliament.
pages.brief: In the House of Lords, some people have titles such as Lord and Lady. Others are important members of the Church of England. The House of Lords works with the House of Commons to make laws. When everyone agrees, the laws become Acts of Parliament.

pages.text: An Amazing Clock Big Ben’s clock tells exactly the right time. People take good care of it. It takes a long time to clean the clock faces. People clean them every five years with soap and water. With its four faces, Big Ben is the biggest chiming clock in the world.
pages.brief: Big Ben’s clock tells exactly the right time, and people take good care of it. Cleaning the clock faces takes a long time. People clean them every five years with soap and water. With its four faces, Big Ben is the biggest chiming clock in the world.

pages.text: People who live in the United Kingdom can go to the top of the Elizabeth Tower and see Big Ben. There, they also get a great view of London and can see how the clocks work. Anyone can go to the Houses of Parliament, though. Everyone can take pictures of the clock tower from the outside.
pages.brief: People who live in the United Kingdom can go to the top of the Elizabeth Tower and see Big Ben. There they get a great view of London and can see how the clocks work. Anyone can go to the Houses of Parliament, and everyone can take pictures of the clock tower from outside.

pages.text: Every New Year’s Eve, there is a huge fireworks show when Big Ben finishes chiming at midnight. Many people come from all over the United Kingdom to see the show. Big Ben always looks amazing on that night.
pages.brief: On New Year’s Eve, a huge fireworks show fills the sky when Big Ben finishes chiming at midnight. Many people come from all over the United Kingdom to see the show. Big Ben looks amazing on that night.

pages.text: Ben the Unstoppable Big Ben is important to the British people. They hear its chimes every day on the radio and television. When bombs damaged one of Big Ben’s clock faces, the bells kept on chiming. Big Ben never stops!
pages.brief: Big Ben is important to the British people. They hear its chimes every day on the radio and television. When bombs damaged one of Big Ben’s clock faces, the bells kept on chiming. Big Ben never stops.

books.title: Ghost Towns
books.art_why: Ghost towns are real places that exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: A Deserted Town Ghost towns are empty places where people once lived. People often leave these towns because of some threat or because they can no longer find work. Each town has a story to tell.
pages.brief: An empty town street with deserted wooden buildings and no people. Doors and windows are closed, and dust or sand lies on the ground. The town was once lived in, but people left because of a threat or because they could no longer find work.

pages.text: Ghost Towns Around the World '3 NORTH AMERICA ASIA '2 EUROPE '0 '4 '2 ATLANTIC OCEAN AFRICA PACIFIC OCEAN INDIAN OCEAN SOUTH AMERICA AUSTRALIA '5 Craco, Italy, page 9 Kayakoy, Turkey, page 3 Centralia, Pennsylvania, page '0 Bannack, Montana, page 4 Okuma, Japan, page '2 (main) Kolmanskop (KOHL-mun-skop), Namibia, page 6 Pripyat, Ukraine, page '2 (sidebar) Grytviken (GRIT-vee-kuhn), St. Kilda, Scotland, page '3 South Georgia, page 7 Ordos, China, page '4 Plymouth, Montserrat Villa Epecuen (VEE-yuh e-pe- (mon-sur-RAT), page 8 KWEN), Argentina, page '5 As shown on the map above, empty towns are found around the world. Imagine what life was like for the people who lived in these places. Why do people leave these towns?
pages.brief: A world map shows continents and oceans. Empty towns are located in many different countries across North America, Asia, Europe, Africa, South America, and Australia. The map suggests that ghost towns exist all around the world.

pages.text: Germans built the town after someone found a diamond (top). Today, the buildings are full of sand (bottom). Resources Vanish Sometimes people leave a town after they run out of a resource. In 1908, a diamond was found in a desert in Africa. Soon after, a new town was born. Everyone left when the diamonds became hard to find.
pages.brief: In a desert in Africa, German settlers build a new town after a diamond is found in 1908. Below, the same town today: empty buildings half-buried in sand, with no people left after diamonds become hard to find.

pages.text: In the 1900s, many people hunted whales around this island. Whales became harder to find over time. Then people stopped hunting whales. People left the town. Old buildings and boats are still there.
pages.brief: On a remote island around the 1900s, people hunt whales from boats near the shore. Later, the island town stands empty; old buildings and wooden boats remain, with no people, after whales become harder to find and whaling stops.

pages.text: Forces of Nature Some places become ghost towns because of natural events. In 1995, a volcano erupted on this Caribbean island. The capital city was almost destroyed. Over half the people who lived on the island have left. The volcano is still active today.
pages.brief: A volcano erupts on a Caribbean island in 1995, sending ash and smoke over the capital city. Damaged buildings stand near the active volcano. Many people have left the island, and the volcano still smokes today.

pages.text: A ghost town in Italy sits on a tall cliff. People in the village left because of earthquakes and landslides. In the 1960s and 1970s, landslides almost destroyed the whole village. The people who still lived there moved away.
pages.brief: An Italian village sits on a tall cliff, with stone buildings packed close together. Earthquakes and landslides in the 1960s and 1970s damage the village. The remaining people move away, leaving the cliffside town empty.

pages.text: Deadly Land People leave some places after the land turns deadly. A town in Pennsylvania is almost completely empty. One day in 1962, the town dump was set on fire to clean up for a holiday. The fire spread into the old mines below the dump, and no one could stop it.
pages.brief: In a Pennsylvania town in 1962, people set the town dump on fire to clean up for a holiday. Flames spread into old mines beneath the dump. The town becomes almost completely empty because no one can stop the fire.

pages.text: After many years, the fire started to burn under the town. Deadly gas went into people’s homes, and holes opened up in the ground. Almost everyone left. The fire will burn for a long time.
pages.brief: Under a Pennsylvania town, an underground mine fire burns for years. Deadly gas seeps into homes, and holes open in the ground. Almost everyone leaves the town. The fire continues to burn underground and will burn for a long time.

pages.text: Water can be as deadly as fire. A large earthquake hit off the coast of Japan in March 2011. The earthquake caused huge waves that hit a nuclear power plant. Harmful radiation filled the air. Thousands of people had to move away. No one knows when—or if— anyone can go back. Chernobyl Disaster Japan isn’t the only country with a ghost town caused by a nuclear accident. A city in Ukraine was home to the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant’s workers and their families. People left the city after a deadly nuclear accident in 1986.
pages.brief: A large earthquake off Japan’s coast in March 2011 sends huge waves toward a nuclear power plant. Harmful radiation fills the air. Thousands of people move away from the town. In Ukraine, a workers’ city near Chernobyl stands empty after a deadly nuclear accident in 1986.

pages.text: A Hard Way of Life People leave some places because they are too hard to get to. In this group of small islands, people couldn’t grow enough food or heat their homes. Young people moved away. Others died because of poor health or old age. The last people moved away in 1930.
pages.brief: On a group of small islands, people struggle to grow enough food and heat their homes. Young people move away. Others die from poor health or old age. The last people leave in 1930, leaving the islands empty.

pages.text: A Brand-New Ghost Town Most ghost towns are not empty from the start. People found coal in an area of China in the early 2000s. A city was built nearby, and people were expected to move there. The new city has always been empty. It is the world’s largest ghost town.
pages.brief: In an area of China in the early 2000s, coal is found. A brand-new city is built nearby, and people are expected to move there. The city has always been empty and becomes the world’s largest ghost town.

pages.text: Empty Places Ghost towns can be old or new, and they are created in many different ways. However, they all have one thing in common: they are lonely places with secrets to share. Think About It Think about cities and towns you have lived in or visited. Hundreds of years from now, some of these places may be ghost towns. What might happen to make people leave?
pages.brief: Old ruins, abandoned streets, and new empty buildings show ghost towns that can be old or new. They are lonely places with secrets. Readers are invited to imagine towns they know becoming empty hundreds of years from now.

books.title: Coins Count
books.art_why: The book shows real children, coins, and shopping items that can be photographed.

pages.text: Counting Dimes and Pennies Kiyana is going shopping. She shakes dimes and pennies out of her bank. Her friend José will help her count how much money she has. José puts the coins in a row and counts.
pages.brief: Kiyana and José are indoors. Kiyana shakes dimes and pennies out of her bank. José puts the coins in a row and counts them. Kiyana is getting ready to go shopping, and José is helping her find out how much money she has.

pages.text: Kiyana shows José an easier way to count the money. She organizes the coins by value. She puts the dimes together. Then Kiyana puts the pennies together. Pennies Dimes Kiyana starts with the dimes. Skip-counting by tens is easy. When she runs out of dimes, she counts the value of the pennies by ones. Kiyana has thirty-five cents in all.
pages.brief: Kiyana shows José an easier way to count the money. She organizes the coins by value, putting the dimes together and the pennies together. Kiyana starts with the dimes and skip-counts by tens. When the dimes are gone, she counts the pennies by ones. She has thirty-five cents in all.

pages.text: Kiyana finds some more pennies in her pocket. She and José don’t want to count all the pennies one by one. So, they decide to count another way. They put the pennies together with the money they have already counted. They will start again from the beginning.
pages.brief: Kiyana finds more pennies in her pocket. She and José do not want to count all the pennies one by one. They decide to count another way. They put the new pennies together with the money they have already counted, then start again from the beginning.

pages.text: Kiyana and José put the coins in groups that are each worth ten cents. Ten pennies have the same value as one dime. They put one dime or ten pennies in each group. Kiyana starts again. This time, she counts her coins by ten. Kiyana has fifty cents in all.
pages.brief: Kiyana and José put the coins into groups that are each worth ten cents. Ten pennies have the same value as one dime. They place one dime or ten pennies in each group. Kiyana starts again and counts the coins by ten. She has fifty cents in all.

pages.text: Counting Dimes and Nickels José is also getting ready to go shopping. He checks to see how much money he has in his bank. He finds nickels and dimes. Kiyana will help José count his coins.
pages.brief: José is getting ready to go shopping. He checks his bank to see how much money he has. Inside, he finds nickels and dimes. Kiyana is nearby and will help José count his coins together.

pages.text: José and Kiyana think about which coins to count first. They start with the dimes because these coins are greater in value. José counts the coins one at a time.
pages.brief: José and Kiyana think about which coins to count first. They start with the dimes because dimes are greater in value. José counts the coins one at a time, placing each dime as he goes.

pages.text: José looks in all his pockets. He finds some more nickels. He decides to start again and to count all his money together. This time, he organizes his coins in groups that are each worth ten cents. Two nickels have the same value as one dime. José puts one dime or two nickels in each group. Why do you think José doesn’t make all the groups worth five cents?
pages.brief: José looks in all his pockets and finds more nickels. He decides to start again and count all his money together. He organizes the coins into groups that are each worth ten cents. Two nickels have the same value as one dime, so he puts one dime or two nickels in each group.

pages.text: José knows you can’t make each group worth five cents. You can’t break a dime in half. This is why he makes each group worth ten cents. José has eighty cents in all.
pages.brief: José knows he cannot make each group worth five cents, because a dime cannot be broken in half. That is why he makes every group worth ten cents. He arranges the groups and finds he has eighty cents in all.

pages.text: Counting Dimes, Nickels, and Pennies Tony is going shopping, too. He shakes dimes, nickels, and pennies out of his bank. Tony organizes his coins from greatest in value to least. Count on This! • Dimes are greater in value than nickels. • Nickels are greater in value than pennies. The order from greatest in value to least is dimes, nickels, pennies. He counts the value of his coins one by one. How much money does Tony have in all?
pages.brief: Tony is going shopping too. He shakes dimes, nickels, and pennies out of his bank. Tony organizes the coins from greatest in value to least: dimes, then nickels, then pennies. He counts the value of the coins one by one to find how much money he has in all.

pages.text: Counting Quarters, Dimes, Nickels, and Pennies Leara has saved quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies. She wants to organize her coins by their value. How would she organize her coins?
pages.brief: Leara has saved quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies. She wants to organize her coins by their value. She looks at the four kinds of coins and decides how to put them in order by value.

pages.text: Count on This! • Quarters are greater in value than dimes. • Dimes are greater in value than nickels. • Nickels are greater in value than pennies. The order from greatest in value to least is quarters, dimes, nickels, pennies.
pages.brief: A close view shows four kinds of coins grouped separately: quarters, then dimes, then nickels, then pennies. The groups are placed in a row from greatest value to least, making the order clear for comparing.

pages.text: Tony has a way for Leara to count. He shows her how to organize her coins by groups that are each worth twenty-five cents. Two dimes and a nickel have the same value as one quarter. So do five nickels. How many pennies would make up a group with a value of twenty-five cents?
pages.brief: Tony shows Leara a way to count her coins. He organizes them into groups that are each worth twenty-five cents. Two dimes and a nickel have the same value as one quarter. Five nickels do too. Tony asks how many pennies would make a group worth twenty-five cents.

pages.text: Leara decides to try a different way to count. She will group as she goes. Leara puts down three quarters. Then she adds a nickel. This group has a value that is a round number. It will be easier to count on from a ten. Next, she counts the dimes. She can skip-count by tens from eighty.
pages.brief: Leara tries a different way to count. She groups as she goes. She puts down three quarters, then adds a nickel. This group has a value that is a round number, making it easier to count on from a ten. Next, she counts the dimes and skip-counts by tens from eighty.

pages.text: Finally, Leara groups the nickels in pairs. Each pair is worth ten cents. So, she can keep on counting by tens. Just the pennies are left. Leara counts on by ones. Leara has $1.33 in all. She and Tony have picked two ways to count these coins. But other ways to count might work faster or better with other groups of coins.
pages.brief: Leara finally groups the nickels in pairs. Each pair is worth ten cents, so she can keep counting by tens. Just the pennies are left, and Leara counts on by ones. She has $1.33 in all. She and Tony have picked two ways to count these coins.

pages.text: Using the Exact Amount José, Kiyana, Tony, and Leara are planning a party. They buy surprises to give to their guests. Kiyana buys a box of buttons for her little brother. It costs thirty-eight cents. She uses three dimes and eight pennies to pay for the buttons. Kiyana has paid for the buttons with the exact amount of money.
pages.brief: José, Kiyana, Tony, and Leara are planning a party and buying surprises for their guests. Kiyana buys a box of buttons for her little brother. It costs thirty-eight cents. She pays with three dimes and eight pennies, using the exact amount.

pages.text: Counting Change José finds a surprise for his little sister. She loves puppies. José finds a puppy picture for her. It costs fifty-eight cents. José has four dimes and eight nickels in his pocket. He has eighty cents in all. He uses all eight nickels and two of his dimes to pay for the picture. These coins have a value of sixty cents. 58¢.
pages.brief: José finds a puppy picture for his little sister, who loves puppies. The picture costs fifty-eight cents. José has four dimes and eight nickels in his pocket, eighty cents in all. He pays with all eight nickels and two dimes, coins worth sixty cents.

pages.text: José pays with sixty cents, but the picture costs just fifty-eight cents. José gets back two pennies. That is his change. The value of the picture plus the change is equal to the sixty cents that José pays. Remember that José started out with four dimes and eight nickels in his pocket. Could he have paid for the picture with four dimes and four nickels instead of the coins he used?
pages.brief: José holds the puppy picture and receives two pennies back as change after paying sixty cents. The picture costs fifty-eight cents. Nearby, his four dimes and eight nickels show the money he started with in his pocket.

pages.text: 43¢ Making Change in Different Ways Tony finds a little mouse for his cat Sparky. He uses five dimes to pay for the mouse. These coins have a value of fifty cents.
pages.brief: Tony holds a little toy mouse for his cat Sparky and pays with five dimes. The five dimes are laid out together, showing a value of fifty cents. Sparky is nearby, waiting for the new toy.

pages.text: The toy mouse costs forty-three cents. Tony pays fifty cents. Count on from forty-three cents to find out how much change Tony gets. 43¢ The value of the mouse plus the seven pennies of change is equal to the fifty cents that Tony paid. Tony could have gotten a nickel and two pennies back as change instead of the seven pennies. Seven pennies have the same value as one nickel and two pennies.
pages.brief: Tony holds the toy mouse that costs forty-three cents. He paid fifty cents, and seven pennies are set out as his change. Beside them, a nickel and two pennies show another way to make the same seven-cent change.

pages.text: 57¢ Leara finds a hat for her sister. It costs fifty-seven cents. She pays for it with three quarters. That is seventy-five cents. She can’t pay with just two quarters because fifty cents is less than the price of the hat.
pages.brief: Leara holds a hat for her sister. The hat costs fifty-seven cents. Leara pays with three quarters, which are laid out to show seventy-five cents. Two quarters would be only fifty cents, less than the price of the hat.

pages.text: Leara gets back a dime, a nickel, and three pennies in change. Is that the right change? The hat costs fifty-seven cents. Leara counts on from fifty-seven cents until she gets to the amount she paid. That amount is three quarters, or seventy-five cents. The value of the hat plus the change is equal to the three quarters that Leara paid. What other groups of coins could be used to make change for Leara?
pages.brief: Leara holds the hat and looks at her change: a dime, a nickel, and three pennies. The hat costs fifty-seven cents, and she paid seventy-five cents. The coins show the change from fifty-seven cents up to seventy-five cents.

pages.text: The day of the party arrives! Tony, Leara, Kiyana, and José give out the presents. Their guests are very happy. And the kids are happy they could count coins to buy the presents.
pages.brief: At the party, Tony, Leara, Kiyana, and José give out the presents to their guests. The guests smile happily as they receive the surprises. The four kids look pleased, knowing they counted coins to buy the presents.

books.title: William Shakespeare
books.art_why: A book about a named famous person, William Shakespeare, so cartoon art fits.

pages.text: Introduction William Shakespeare was a poet and a playwright in England. He was born in 1564. He died in 1616. Shakespeare has been a popular writer for more than four hundred years. People like his plays because they make people feel happy, sad, shocked, or scared. His stories are exciting, and they also make people think about big ideas such as good and evil. Writers still look to his beautiful writing to help them write their own good stories.
pages.brief: A cartoon William Shakespeare stands in England holding a quill and a page of a play. Around him small groups of people laugh, look sad, look shocked and look scared at his stories, and he is thinking about big ideas like good and evil as he writes.

pages.text: Shakespeare’s Family William was born to John and Mary Shakespeare in England in April 1564. He probably went to a very good school as a boy. Most people at the time didn’t know how to read or write. Shakespeare married a woman named Anne in 1582. They had three children.
pages.brief: In England in April 1564, a baby William is shown with his parents John and Mary Shakespeare. A schoolroom shows him as a boy at a good school, while other people nearby cannot read or write. Later, grown-up William stands with his wife Anne and their three children.

pages.text: Shakespeare in London By 1592, Shakespeare moved to London and worked as an actor and playwright. Soon after, he had become part owner of an acting group. Shakespeare rose to success. In 1599, he helped found a popular London theater.
pages.brief: In London in 1592, Shakespeare acts on a stage and writes a play. He is shown as part owner of an acting group, standing with other actors. In 1599 he helps found a popular London theater, shown as a building going up with people around it.

pages.text: London Theater Theater was exciting during Shakespeare’s time, with fancy costumes and sword fights. The crowds were loud. They yelled “boo” at the bad guys and cheered the good guys. They even threw food at the actors. Most plays took place in the afternoon under natural daylight. Only men were allowed to act. Women were banned from acting.
pages.brief: An afternoon open-air theater in London: actors in fancy costumes sword-fight on stage under natural daylight, all of them men. A loud crowd yells at the bad guy and cheers the good guy, and someone throws food at the actors.

pages.text: Shakespeare’s Plays Shakespeare wrote three main types of plays: tragedies, histories, and comedies. Tragedies are sad plays with people who make mistakes.
pages.brief: A writer's table with three kinds of plays laid out. A tragedy scene shows a sad character who has made a mistake, looking upset while the people around him suffer.

pages.text: Shakespeare’s history plays are mostly about kings of England. Shakespeare’s comedies are often funny love stories.
pages.brief: Two play scenes side by side: a history play showing kings of England on thrones, and a comedy showing a funny love story with a smiling couple.

pages.text: Shakespeare’s Importance For hundreds of years, people around the world have enjoyed Shakespeare’s plays. They’ve laughed and cried along with his characters. Shakespeare’s stories are just as good as time passes.
pages.brief: Crowds of people around the world, shown in different places, watch Shakespeare's plays. Some laugh and some cry along with his characters, and the scenes show that his stories stay good as time passes.

pages.text: People feel connected to Shakespeare’s stories about love, hate, bravery, and power. It doesn’t matter if they take place today or long ago. People relate to his characters. For example, Iago from Othello is evil yet still human. Shakespeare’s characters Romeo and Juliet stand the test of time as an example of true love.
pages.brief: People are drawn to Shakespeare's stories about love, hate, bravery and power. Iago from Othello is shown as an evil man who still looks human, and Romeo and Juliet stand together as an example of true love.

pages.text: People around the world can read Shakespeare’s plays in their own language. Shakespeare festivals around the world draw large crowds. Some actors are even doing the plays in the kind of English from Shakespeare’s time. It sounds much different from today’s English. Many actors say that their parts in Shakespeare’s plays are the most important they’ve ever played. Actors have to work really hard to become their characters. Children act in his plays as well. Many of Shakespeare’s plays have been made into films.
pages.brief: People around the world read Shakespeare's plays in their own languages, and big festival crowds gather. Actors speak the old English of Shakespeare's time, work hard to become their characters, and children act too. A film camera shows one play being made into a film.

pages.text: Shakespeare’s Poems Shakespeare wrote one hundred fifty- four sonnets. A sonnet is a special type of poem with fourteen lines. His sonnets were mostly about love. His most famous sonnet began with the line, “Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?” Language Wizard.
pages.brief: Shakespeare sits writing his sonnets, a stack of one hundred fifty-four beside him. One sonnet of fourteen lines is shown mostly about love, and a summer's day is pictured beside the famous opening line.

pages.text: Shakespeare’s Death William Shakespeare died in 1616. His friends put together a book of his plays. They made sure that people read and saw his plays. His friend wrote about Shakespeare’s work in the book. He said it was “for all time.” He was right!
pages.brief: William Shakespeare dies in 1616. His friends gather to put together a book of his plays so people will read and see them, and one friend writes about Shakespeare's work in the book, calling it for all time.

pages.text: Conclusion Today, William Shakespeare is thought to be one of the greatest writers who ever lived. Shakespeare’s plays are exciting and fun, and they also touch people. His characters show how difficult—and how beautiful—life can be.
pages.brief: William Shakespeare is shown today as one of the greatest writers who ever lived. His plays are exciting and fun and touch people, and his characters show how difficult and how beautiful life can be.

books.title: United Arab Emirates
books.art_why: The UAE, its people, cities, and landmarks exist today, so photographs are possible.

pages.text: Where Is It? The United Arab Emirates (UAE) is a small country in the Middle East. The Middle East is the area where Europe, Africa, and Asia meet. The UAE’s coast runs along a gulf that connects to the Indian Ocean.
pages.brief: A wide view shows the small country of the United Arab Emirates in the Middle East, at the meeting point of Europe, Africa, and Asia. Its coastline runs along a gulf that connects to the Indian Ocean.

pages.text: The UAE is made up of seven Arab states. The capital city is Abu Dhabi. The city is old. Its history dates back to 3,000 bce. Modern Abu Dhabi blends old customs with modern buildings.
pages.brief: Abu Dhabi, the capital city, appears with old buildings beside modern towers. The city’s long history reaches back to 3,000 BCE, and the scene blends old customs with modern buildings. The country is made up of seven Arab states.

pages.text: People Millions of people call the UAE home. Most of the people who live there are from other countries. They came to work or to build new buildings. The people of the UAE come from different Arab groups. Those groups settled in the area long ago. Many people share customs and wear Arab clothing. Men and women wear scarves and cover their heads. They do this to respect their religion.
pages.brief: Many people from different countries live in the UAE, some having come to work or build new buildings. People from different Arab groups share customs and wear Arab clothing. Men and women wear scarves and cover their heads to show respect for their religion.

pages.text: Most of the people of the UAE also share the religion of Islam. Arabic is the main language, but many people speak local languages. Most people live in cities and towns along the UAE coast. Oil has made the country rich. It has turned poor UAE villages into modern cities.
pages.brief: Most people live in cities and towns along the UAE coast. Arabic is the main language, and many people speak local languages. Oil has made the country rich and has turned poor villages into modern cities.

pages.text: Land On the coast, the UAE is hot. The country gets little rain. In the east are the tall Hajar Mountains. A little rain falls in the mountains. Inland, the UAE is mostly made up of desert. There it is even hotter. In summer or winter, wind may carry dust and sand. The wind creates huge sand hills.
pages.brief: On the hot coast, the UAE gets little rain. In the east rise the tall Hajar Mountains, where a little rain falls. Inland is mostly desert, even hotter, where wind carries dust and sand and creates huge sand hills.

pages.text: Only a few grasses and bushes grow in most parts of the desert. There is more water in an oasis. Plants and animals can live there. Dates, grain, mangoes, and other foods grow in an oasis. These spots also help animals live.
pages.brief: Only a few grasses and bushes grow in most of the desert. An oasis holds more water, so plants and animals can live there. Dates, grain, mangoes, and other foods grow in the oasis, and these spots help animals live.

pages.text: History People have lived in the UAE for thousands of years. The area has always been important for trade. In the 1800s, Great Britain took over the states to control trade. They traded for things such as tea and silk from Asia. Though trade passed through the states, most villages stayed poor for hundreds of years. In 1958, people looking for oil found it in the Middle East. They quickly began drilling to get the oil.
pages.brief: For thousands of years the area was important for trade. In the 1800s, Great Britain took over the states to control trade in goods such as tea and silk from Asia. Most villages stayed poor for hundreds of years until oil was found in 1958 and drilling began.

pages.text: The British ruled the area for hundreds of years. In 1968, the states decided to form one country. When all seven states joined, the UAE was free from Britain. The country grew rich with its oil.
pages.brief: The British ruled the area for hundreds of years. In 1968 the states decided to form one country, and when all seven states joined, the UAE was free from Britain. The country grew rich with its oil.

pages.text: Landmarks The Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque is one of the most beautiful UAE buildings. The mosque is important to the religion of Islam. Islam teaches respect, peace, and love. The Burj Khalifa in Dubai sets the record as the tallest building in the world. It stands for everything that is possible in Dubai.
pages.brief: The Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque is one of the most beautiful buildings in the UAE and is important to Islam, which teaches respect, peace, and love. In Dubai, the Burj Khalifa stands as the tallest building in the world and stands for what is possible in Dubai.

pages.text: Another landmark in Dubai is Palm Jumeirah. It is one of the world’s largest man-made islands. From above, it looks like a palm tree.
pages.brief: A view from above shows Palm Jumeirah in Dubai, one of the world’s largest man-made islands. Its shape looks like a palm tree, and this landmark stands in the city as a special place in Dubai.

pages.text: Conclusion The United Arab Emirates is a new country in an old part of the world. Mosques and clothing show its customs. Modern buildings look to tomorrow. The UAE will continue to grow and change.
pages.brief: The United Arab Emirates is a new country in an old part of the world. Mosques and clothing show its customs, while modern buildings look to tomorrow. The UAE will continue to grow and change.

pages.text: United Arab Emirates Population: 5,927,482 Land: 83,600 sq km (32,278 sq. mi.) Capital City: Abu Dhabi Primary Language: Arabic Primary Religion: Islam Name of Currency: UAE dirham.
pages.brief: A broad view of the United Arab Emirates shows Abu Dhabi as its capital city. Arabic is the main language and Islam is the main religion. The country uses the UAE dirham, and its land and population are part of the country today.

books.title: Lice Aren't Nice
books.art_why: Head lice, people, pets, combs, and hair dryers are real things that can be shown in photographs today.

pages.text: Who Gets Head Lice? Head lice love to chomp on human heads. They have bugged people for thousands of years. Yet many people don’t understand what they are or where they come from. Some people think head lice are a sign of a filthy home. Others think only people who don’t wash enough get them.
pages.brief: A magnified head louse clings to a strand of human hair. In the background, children and adults with different hair types stand together, showing that head lice can affect many people. The tiny insect feeds on a human head.

pages.text: From Louse to Lice When you see more than one mouse, you don’t call them mouses, right? You call them mice. In the same way, one of these insects is called a louse, but two or more are called lice. In fact, who gets lice has nothing to do with how clean your home or school is. It’s not about how often you wash or brush your hair. It’s not about your hair length, either. Head lice affect people who are rich and people who are poor. They affect people all over the world. Lice Aren’t Nice.
pages.brief: One small louse clings to a hair beside two lice on a nearby hair. Below, children with long and short hair, from different homes, stand together in a clean classroom, showing that head lice affect rich and poor people all over the world.

pages.text: Name That Louse! Different types of lice live on humans. They all feed on human blood. Body lice and head lice look almost the same, but head lice are a bit smaller. An adult head louse is about the size of a pencil point!
pages.brief: A magnified photograph compares a body louse and a head louse side by side on human skin. The head louse is slightly smaller. A pencil point rests nearby to show that an adult head louse is about that tiny size.

pages.text: Their small size makes them tough to spot and tough to catch. Strong claws on their legs help them hold tight to human hair. Lice Aren’t Nice.
pages.brief: A magnified photograph of a head louse gripping human hair with strong claws. Its small body is hard to spot among strands of hair. A hand holds a strand of hair close, showing how tightly the louse can hold on.

pages.text: How Do We Get Head Lice? Head lice usually spread when people touch heads. Sometimes they spread when a person with head lice shares a hat, comb, or other item. A louse can hitch a ride on the shared item to reach a new person.
pages.brief: Two children sit close together, their heads touching, while a tiny louse moves from one child’s hair to the other. Nearby, a shared hat and comb rest on a table, showing how a louse can hitch a ride to a new person.

pages.text: Pet Pests? Cats and dogs can get lice, too. However, their lice are different from the kind that like human hair. Cats and dogs can’t give us their lice, and we can’t give them ours, either. If your pet does get lice, get him or her to a vet! Head lice can’t live for long away from a human body, however. If one crawls onto something like a comb, it usually dies before reaching another person. Lice Aren’t Nice.
pages.brief: A cat and a dog sit with a child. A veterinarian gently checks the dog’s fur, while a magnified pet louse is shown apart from a human head louse. A comb on a table has a louse on it.

pages.text: Head Lice Life Head lice eggs, called nits, are tiny. They attach to hairs with special glue that makes them hard to remove. In order to hatch, nits need to stay close to the scalp to stay warm. They are usually found near the scalp, often near the ears and back of the head.
pages.brief: A close-up photograph of a human scalp near the ear and the back of the head. Tiny nits are glued to individual hairs close to the scalp. A hand parts the hair to show the small eggs stuck firmly in place.

pages.text: Head Louse Life Cycle After they hatch, the young lice must feed within twenty-four hours to stay alive. They become adults in about ten to twelve days. Along the way, they outgrow the hard outer layer that helps protect their bodies. When they grow too large, they shed the outer layer and grow a new one. Lice Aren’t Nice.
pages.brief: A magnified photograph shows a tiny young louse newly hatched from a nit on a human hair. Nearby, an adult louse has shed its hard outer layer, leaving the old casing behind as it grows a new one.

pages.text: Head lice have pointed, straw-like mouths for sucking blood. Their bites don’t hurt. However, head lice inject a small amount of saliva when they feed. The saliva helps keep blood flowing, which makes it easier to drink. The saliva is also what makes bites red and often itchy.
pages.brief: A magnified photograph of a head louse on human skin, its pointed, straw-like mouth pressed down as it feeds. A small red, itchy bite mark is visible nearby. A tiny drop of saliva is shown entering the skin.

pages.text: Bugs Begone! The first sign of head lice is usually the ticklish feeling of something in your hair. If you have head lice, people can sometimes spot nits in your hair. Spotting head lice is hard, though. They don’t like light and can crawl quickly to avoid it. Sometimes people use a “lice comb” with very fine teeth to aid the search. Lice Aren’t Nice.
pages.brief: A child sits still while an adult parts the child’s hair with a fine-toothed lice comb, searching close to the scalp. The child’s hand is raised to scratch a ticklish spot. A magnified louse crawls quickly away from the light.

pages.text: Head lice are often killed with chemicals, but there are ways to avoid chemicals. For instance, kids and parents can use a machine like a hair dryer instead. It uses hot air to kill lice and nits.
pages.brief: In a bathroom, an adult aims a hair dryer at a child’s hair, sending hot air through the strands and near the scalp. A bottle of chemical lice treatment is set aside on the counter, showing a way to avoid chemicals.

pages.text: Super Lice! No, these lice aren’t bigger or bloodthirstier than other lice, but they are harder to kill. Certain chemicals we’ve used to kill them in the past no longer do the trick. The Truth About Head Lice Anyone can get head lice. They aren’t a sign of dirty hair or a dirty house. They’re a sign that you’re human. You just need help to get rid of your itchy guests. So spread the word— not the lice! Lice Aren’t Nice.
pages.brief: A magnified photograph shows a head louse on human hair beside a bottle of lice chemical. The louse remains alive, showing it is harder to kill. Nearby, children and adults with different hair types stand together, ready to get help for itchy scalps.

books.title: Teotihuacan
books.art_why: Ancient city from almost two thousand years ago, before photographs existed.

pages.text: A Huge City More than six hundred years ago, a group of Native Americans found a very old city. There were two huge pyramids but no people. No one knows who built the city. They named the city Teotihuacán (tay-oh-tee-wah-KAHN). That was their word for “place where the gods were born.”
pages.brief: A group of Native American travelers stands at the edge of an empty ancient city, facing two huge stone pyramids. No people live among the ruins. The travelers look across the silent ruins and pyramids, discovering the abandoned place more than six hundred years ago.

pages.text: The Center of Teotihuacán The Pyramid of the Moon is 20,280 square meters (217,686 sq. ft.) at the base and rises 43 meters (141 ft.). Pyramid of the Moon Palace Plaza of the Moon Pyramid of the Sun Plaza of the Columns The Avenue of the Dead is as wide as an eleven-lane highway. The Pyramid of the Sun is about 220 by 230 meters (720 by 760 ft.) at the base and is 66 meters (216 ft.) high. Palace Avenue of the Dead Palace Citadel The Citadel measures about 400 meters (1,300 ft.) per side. Temple of the Feathered Serpent.
pages.brief: Wide view of the center of Teotihuacán, with the Pyramid of the Moon and the Pyramid of the Sun rising above plazas, palaces, and the broad Avenue of the Dead. The Citadel and the Temple of the Feathered Serpent stand among the ancient stone structures.

pages.text: The ruins of Teotihuacán are spread over a huge area. A Mysterious City When it was built almost two thousand years ago, Teotihuacán was one of the biggest cities in the world. At that time, most people lived in small communities. What made Teotihuacán grow so big? warrior carving.
pages.brief: The ruins of Teotihuacán spread across a huge open area. In the distance, small early communities sit near the growing city. A carved warrior figure stands among the old stones, showing a clue from the city that became one of the biggest in the world.

pages.text: The people who ruled the great city left few clues about themselves. We do not know who they were. They wrote with pictures, but no one knows how to read the pictures today. Experts must search the area for clues about the people.
pages.brief: An expert kneels among the ruins of Teotihuacán, searching the ground for clues. Nearby, ancient picture symbols appear on weathered stone, but their meaning is lost. The rulers of the great city left few traces of who they were.

pages.text: Clues about the City We know the rulers found a good place for farming. The soil was rich, and water flowed from the mountains. There were caves there, too. Evidence shows that the people believed their gods were born in caves.
pages.brief: People farm in the rich soil beside Teotihuacán, while water flows down from the mountains. Nearby, dark caves open in the land. The people look toward the caves, believing their gods were born inside them, and the good land helps the city.

pages.text: The city grew slowly at first. That changed when two nearby volcanoes erupted. Thousands of people had to run for their lives. Many came to Teotihuacán. These people were from other cultures, but they were welcomed. They helped the city grow.
pages.brief: Two nearby volcanoes erupt, throwing smoke and fire into the sky. Thousands of people run from the danger, carrying what they can. Many arrive at Teotihuacán, where city people welcome them, and the newcomers help the city grow.

pages.text: The new people needed housing. The rulers ordered thousands of new homes built. These homes were unlike any others in the world. At first, experts who found the homes thought they were palaces for rich people. They learned that these homes were for everyone.
pages.brief: Rows of new stone homes fill a neighborhood in Teotihuacán, unlike other homes in the world. Families move in and settle. An expert studies the rows of homes, learning that they were built for everyone, not just rich people.

pages.text: People lived well in the city. The rulers ordered new temples, too. Experts studied the stone statues on the temples. It took many artists to carve them. It took more artists to paint the outside of the temples with bright colors.
pages.brief: Artists carve stone statues on a new temple in Teotihuacán. Others paint the temple outside with bright colors. People live well in the city, and the rulers have ordered new temples built, giving the artists much work to do.

pages.text: A Mysterious Ending As experts continued to explore the site, they found statues that were smashed. Also, temples were burned. The experts learned that the great city was attacked. However, who attacked it remains a mystery. At some point, the people left the city, but no one is sure why. Grasses and other plants slowly covered the city.
pages.brief: Experts explore the ruined city and find smashed statues and burned temples. The great city was attacked, though no one knows who attacked it. The people left at some point, and grasses and other plants slowly cover the empty buildings and stone.

pages.text: The Park Today Today, part of the old city is a national park. Visitors come by the thousands. Many climb to the top of the Pyramid of the Sun. Climbing the 248 steps is scary because they are steep, but the view is great.
pages.brief: Many visitors come to the national park at Teotihuacán. A crowd climbs the steep stone steps of the Pyramid of the Sun, all 248 of them. From the top, the climbers look out over the ancient city and the wide view.

pages.text: A New Threat Wind, rain, and visitors harm Teotihuacán slowly. Today there is a new danger. Buildings are going up very fast. When builders dig near the city, they sometimes find things from the old city. They are asked to hand over what they find, but sometimes they don’t. The clues are lost forever.
pages.brief: Wind and rain wear at the old ruins while visitors walk among them. Nearby, modern buildings go up fast. Builders dig near the city and uncover old objects. Some hand over what they find, but sometimes they do not, and clues are lost forever.

pages.text: New Clues There is a lot to see at Teotihuacán. It is a place of many mysteries. Experts are working to solve them. One expert is Sergio Gómez. One day, Gómez saw a strange hole in the ground. The hole led to a tunnel. With a team of experts, Gómez dug up thousands of new clues. Maybe he will solve some of the mysteries of this special place.
pages.brief: Expert Sergio Gómez stands at a strange hole in the ground at Teotihuacán. The hole leads to a tunnel. With a team of experts, Gómez digs inside and uncovers thousands of new clues, hoping to solve some of the mysteries of this special place.

books.title: Observing Ramadan
books.art_why: Ramadan is observed by real families today, so photographs of homes, meals and communities are the truest pictures.

pages.text: What Is Ramadan? Holidays and other events are often times of celebration. People usually celebrate something about their country or as part of their religion or culture. Ramadan is an important time for Muslims—people who follow the religion of Islam.
