pages.brief: A Muslim family celebrating together indoors, smiling and gesturing warmly in a bright room. Clay lanterns and simple decorations sit nearby, and several generations are gathered as if marking a special occasion, showing that Ramadan is an important time for people who follow Islam.

pages.text: While holidays can last for only a day or two, Ramadan is a whole month long. The date of Ramadan changes from year to year. It depends on a calendar that marks the start of each month with a new moon.
pages.brief: A wall calendar hangs above a table while a thin new moon shows in the darkening evening sky outside the window. The calendar page is turned to a fresh month, suggesting how the start of Ramadan shifts each year and follows a calendar marked by the new moon.

pages.text: Muslims spend a lot of time praying and enjoying time with family while observing Ramadan. This helps Muslims connect with their faith and with their family and community.
pages.brief: A Muslim family prays together on a patterned rug in a bright living room, hands raised and heads bowed. A grandmother and two children kneel nearby, and the closeness of the group shows how praying and spending time with family connect people to their faith and community.

pages.text: Fasting During Ramadan One of the most important parts of Ramadan is fasting. Fasting during Ramadan helps Muslims focus on why their faith is important to them. For the month of Ramadan, many Muslims fast between sunrise and sunset. Once it is dark outside, they eat and drink as usual. Muslims who fast continue to go to school and work.
pages.brief: Two scenes of a fasting day: a man and a teenage girl walking to work and school in the morning light with bags and books, then the same family seated at a table after dark, eating and drinking as usual once the sun has set.

pages.text: Some Muslims choose not to fast during Ramadan. Instead, they donate money, clothes, food, or their time to help people in need. These acts are different ways to spend time thinking about their religion. Thinking about other people’s feelings is an important part of Ramadan. Muslims hold back from arguing and speaking badly about people during the holy month.
pages.brief: Volunteers sort boxes of food, folded clothes and envelopes of money at a community collection point, handing bags to neighbours who need help. One volunteer sits talking kindly with an older man, showing how some Muslims give time and goods instead of fasting.

pages.text: Do You Know? The number of hours that Muslims fast each day during Ramadan isn’t the same in every country. It depends on the time of year when Ramadan falls. The amount of time between sunrise and sunset changes from place to place and from day to day. Most Muslims fast between eleven and sixteen hours a day. However, Muslims who live in areas far north may fast for more than twenty hours. During the summer months, days in the north are long and nights are short. Fasting Hours Around the World NORTH AMERICA EUROPE ASIA AFRICA AUSTRALIA SOUTH AMERICA ANTARCTICA This map shows the number of hours some Muslims around the world fasted during Ramadan in 2019.
pages.brief: A large world map shows the continents, with regions shaded to show how daylight hours differ from place to place. A bright sun hangs over the far north, where summer days are long and nights short, while other areas of the map show shorter daylight.

pages.text: Eating During Ramadan Muslims usually eat two meals a day during Ramadan, one right after sunset and another just before sunrise. Most Muslims wake up before sunrise to eat a meal called suhoor. Coal miners in Turkey take a break to enjoy suhoor underground.
pages.brief: Deep underground in a Turkish coal mine, miners in helmets and dusty work clothes sit on crates eating a pre-sunrise meal by lamplight, taking a break to enjoy suhoor before the day's fast begins above ground.

pages.text: Some people set their alarm clock for before sunrise. Others depend on night callers, people who move through neighborhoods singing songs and hitting drums.
pages.brief: A bedside alarm clock glows before dawn in a dark bedroom. Outside on a narrow street, a night caller walks between houses, singing and striking a drum to wake families for their early meal, his figure lit by a streetlamp.

pages.text: Families enjoy cooking together before sunset to prepare the evening meal, called iftar. In some communities, people give each other food. Before sunset, children visit nearby houses to share food with friends. Then they return home to wait for sundown. In some places, families watch the firing of a cannon on television. It means that the day’s fasting has come to an end.
pages.brief: A family cooks together in a warm kitchen before sunset, stirring pots and setting plates for the evening meal. In another doorway, children carry dishes of food to neighbours' houses, and a television shows a cannon firing to mark the end of the day's fast.

pages.text: In some areas, the middle of Ramadan marks a special time for children. They wear colorful clothes, sing songs, and visit houses to get candy. A clown gives out candy to children in Saudi Arabia on the fifteenth night of Ramadan.
pages.brief: Children in colourful clothes sing and hold out bags of candy on a neighbourhood street in Saudi Arabia. Beside them a clown in costume hands sweets to a laughing girl, marking the special middle night of Ramadan for children.

pages.text: The End of Ramadan The rise of a crescent moon marks the end of Ramadan. Families and friends gather to watch the night sky in search of the Moon. Once they see it, a holiday called Eid al-Fitr begins. Muslims dress up, share meals with family and friends, and give each other gifts.
pages.brief: Families and friends gather on a rooftop at dusk, faces turned up as a thin crescent moon appears between the buildings. Below, people in their best clothes greet one another, share a meal and exchange wrapped gifts as Eid al-Fitr begins.

pages.text: Muslims around the world observe Ramadan in different ways. Many people pray, fast, and spend time with loved ones. Ramadan is a time for Muslims to honor their religion and their community.
pages.brief: A wide view of Muslims around the world: a family praying at home, a father and daughter sharing food, and neighbours greeting one another in a busy street. Together they show people honouring their religion and their community in different ways during Ramadan.

books.title: The Water Cycle
books.art_why: Keyword check indicates a drawing, and the water cycle is shown as a clear process illustration.

pages.text: Water All Around Us Water covers most of Earth. It’s found in lakes, rivers, and oceans. It’s on top of mountains in the form of snow or ice. It’s deep under the ground. Water is even in the air around you.
pages.brief: A wide landscape shows water in many places: a lake, a river, and the ocean, snow and ice on a mountain top, water deep under the ground, and moisture in the air around the land.

pages.text: The water you see today has been around for a long time. Did you drink water this morning? It might be the same water a dinosaur drank a million years ago!
pages.brief: A child holds a glass of water and drinks, while a dinosaur stands beside ancient water and drinks too. The scene links the water the child drinks today with water a dinosaur drank long ago.

pages.text: How is this possible? All water on Earth is recycled! Although you can’t always see it happening, Earth’s water is moving around in a never-ending pattern. This pattern is called the water cycle.
pages.brief: Earth is shown as a whole planet with water moving around it in a continuous, never-ending pattern. The scene shows the recycling of water through the environment, connecting water on land, in the air, and in the oceans.

pages.text: From Liquid to Gas Imagine a puddle of water on a hot day. As the day goes on, the puddle of water gets smaller and smaller until it’s completely gone.
pages.brief: On a hot, sunny day, a puddle of water lies on the ground in the warm air. As the Sun shines down, the puddle gets smaller and smaller until only a small patch of water remains.

pages.text: Although you can’t see it anymore, the water didn’t just go away. The puddle grew smaller because heat from the Sun turned the liquid water into an invisible gas. Do You Know? Sometimes when water is heated up, you might see a cloud rising from it. This cloud is called steam. Steam is a mix of tiny drops of liquid water and water in the form of gas. You can see steam because the drops of water make it visible.
pages.brief: The Sun heats liquid water, turning it into an invisible gas that rises into the air. Near the water, a cloud of steam rises from heated water, made of tiny liquid drops and water gas.

pages.text: This is the first step of the water cycle. It is known as evaporation. Most evaporation on Earth happens in bigger bodies of water, such as rivers, lakes, and the ocean.
pages.brief: The warm Sun shines over a large river, a lake, and the ocean. Water vapor rises slowly from these big bodies of water into the sky, showing the first step of the water cycle, evaporation.

pages.text: Up in the Air When water is in the form of gas, it’s called water vapor. Air carries the water vapor high into the sky. As water vapor rises, it cools and becomes tiny droplets of liquid water. Then, the water droplets form clouds. This step of the water cycle is called condensation.
pages.brief: Air carries water vapor high into the sky above the ground. As the vapor rises, it cools and becomes tiny droplets of liquid water. These droplets come together and form clouds, showing the step called condensation.

pages.text: Sometimes water droplets in the clouds grow too big and heavy for the air to hold. When this happens, they fall back down to Earth as rain, snow, sleet, or hail. This step of the cycle is known as precipitation.
pages.brief: Heavy clouds fill the sky over the land. Water droplets inside have grown too big and heavy for the air to hold, so they fall back down to Earth as rain, snow, sleet, and hail.

pages.text: Where Does It All Go? Sometimes the water that falls to Earth flows across the ground. After a while, it collects in rivers and streams that carry it to the ocean. This step of the water cycle is called runoff. Runoff is important because it carries water back to the ocean and keeps the water cycle going.
pages.brief: Water falls to Earth and flows steadily across the ground. It collects in a river and a stream, which carry the water toward the wide ocean. This movement shows runoff keeping the water cycle going.

pages.text: Other times, the water soaks into the ground. This water is called groundwater. Groundwater helps us grow our food and is also an important supply of water we can drink. A lot of this water also keeps moving underground and later reaches the ocean.
pages.brief: Water soaks into the ground and becomes groundwater. Deep below the surface, groundwater helps plants grow above and keeps moving underground toward the ocean. It is also an important supply of water people can drink.

pages.text: The Water Cycle Is Important The water that falls from the sky makes its way into oceans, rivers, streams, and lakes. From there, the cycle starts all over again with evaporation!
pages.brief: Water falls from the sky and makes its way into oceans, rivers, streams, and lakes. From these bodies of water, the Sun heats the water again, and the water cycle starts all over with evaporation.

pages.text: The water cycle helps life on Earth. Without it, lakes and rivers would dry up. Rain would stop falling from the sky. Plants wouldn’t be able to grow. There would be no water for people and other animals to drink. The water cycle helps make Earth a healthy planet. Water is truly amazing!
pages.brief: A healthy Earth shows the water cycle helping life. Rain falls, lakes and rivers hold water, plants grow, and people and animals have water to drink. The scene shows a healthy planet where water supports life everywhere.

books.title: The Gray Wolf
books.art_why: Keyword check suggests drawing; this book uses that style.

pages.text: Introduction Gray wolves are mammals with thick fur and long, bushy tails. The largest of all wolves, gray wolves are predators that can survive in many areas. They live on mountains and in forests and deserts.
pages.brief: A gray wolf with thick fur and a long, bushy tail stands on a rocky mountain slope, with forest and desert terrain visible in the distance; other gray wolves are nearby, showing that they can survive in many areas.

pages.text: Wolf Features Adult gray wolves are usually just under a meter (3 ft.) tall at the shoulder. From their nose to tail, they are almost 2 meters (more than 6 ft.) long. A male wolf weighs around 45 kilograms (100 lb.) but can weigh as much as 65 kilograms (143 lb.). Female wolves are smaller. Gray wolves are fierce predators. They can run fast and have powerful jaws with sharp teeth.
pages.brief: An adult male gray wolf stands beside a smaller female, showing his long body from nose to tail and powerful jaws with sharp teeth; he is large and heavy, and he runs fast while the smaller female wolf watches.

pages.text: Gray wolves are not just gray. Their fur can have many colors, from white to black.
pages.brief: Several gray wolves stand together, their thick fur showing a range of colors from white through gray to black; one wolf is pale and another is dark, making clear that gray wolves are not just gray.

pages.text: Wolf Packs Wolves are social animals. They live in groups called packs. A pack usually has six to ten wolves. Wolves have been known to travel in packs of up to thirty.
pages.brief: A group of gray wolves moves together as a pack, with six to ten wolves close together and more wolves visible farther back, showing that wolves are social animals and can travel in packs of up to thirty.

pages.text: The pack is made up of one male leader, one female leader, and their offspring. The male and female leaders are called alphas. Each wolf has a rank or position in the pack, with the alpha male at the top.
pages.brief: A gray wolf pack is shown with one male leader and one female leader at the front and their offspring behind; the alpha male stands at the top of the group, with each wolf in a clear rank below him.

pages.text: Working in packs helps wolves hunt large animals such as deer, elk, and moose. They also hunt smaller animals such as rabbits. Wolves sometimes follow groups of large animals for days. They look for weak or hurt animals. Then they hide and surround a target. When the leader signals, the wolves attack.
pages.brief: Several gray wolves work together to hunt large animals, hiding and surrounding a large elk while a deer and a moose stand nearby; a rabbit is also nearby, and the wolf leader signals the pack to attack after following the animals.

pages.text: Pack members use all five of their senses to communicate with each other. They change the positions of their ears and tails to mean different things. They also bark, cry, and howl, as well as smell and lick each other, to communicate. Do You Know? Every gray wolf’s howl sounds different.
pages.brief: A group of gray wolves communicates using all five senses: one changes the position of its ears and tail, another barks and howls, and two smell and lick each other; every wolf’s howl sounds different from the next.

pages.text: Wolf Pups Between January and April, the alphas mate. Around sixty days later, the female digs a long tunnel with a den at the end. In the den, she gives birth to four to six pups. The pups are born blind and deaf. They weigh only about as much as a can of soup.
pages.brief: A female gray wolf digs a long tunnel with a den at the end, and inside the den four to six tiny pups lie blind and deaf, each about as small as a can of soup.

pages.text: The pups nurse for about two months. Then they enjoy warm meals of meat that their parents regurgitate for them. The offspring stay with the pack until they are at least two years old. Then they leave to look for mates.
pages.brief: A female gray wolf nurses her pups, and the parents regurgitate warm meat for them; older offspring stay close to the pack until they are at least two years old, then leave to look for mates.

pages.text: Wolf Territory Long ago, the sound of a gray wolf’s howl would often break the quiet of the night. Gray wolves once roamed freely around the world. However, over the past hundred years, they have lost much of their territory. Gray Wolves on the Rise By 1926, gray wolves had been killed off in Yellowstone National Park, in the United States. A program started in 1995 brought wolves back to the park. Scientists wanted the wolves to help keep the numbers of elk in the park under control. In 2016, around one hundred wolves lived in the park. Their numbers continue to grow.
pages.brief: At night, a gray wolf howls in the quiet, and gray wolves roam freely in Yellowstone National Park; after a 1995 program brings wolves back to the park, around one hundred wolves live there by 2016, with elk nearby and scientists watching the growing numbers.

pages.text: As people built new towns and cities, they changed the land. They drove the wolves away. People also hunted wolves to keep them from killing their cattle and sheep. Over time, the numbers of gray wolves in Europe and the United States dropped. Today, their numbers are on the rise again in some places.
pages.brief: People build new towns and cities, changing the land and driving gray wolves away; people also hunt wolves to protect cattle and sheep, and over time wolf numbers drop in Europe and the United States, though today they are on the rise in some places.

pages.text: Conclusion Gray wolves have lost a lot of territory, but now they are getting some of it back. Gray wolves are social animals. A pack of gray wolves lives and hunts together. As top predators, gray wolves are important to the balance of our natural world.
pages.brief: A pack of gray wolves lives and hunts together in the natural world, with some wolves returning to land they lost; as top predators, they stand at the center of the scene, showing their importance to the balance of nature.

books.title: Insect Life Cycle
books.art_why: Insects are real animals that can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction When you were born, your body was shaped a lot like it is now. It was smaller, of course, but you had a head, legs, arms, and a torso. When you grow up, your body shape will be about the same. But some baby animals look nothing like the adults they will become.
pages.brief: A human baby and a grown adult stand side by side on a plain background, the baby smaller but with the same head, arms, legs, and torso shape. Nearby, a baby animal and its grown adult form are shown with very different body shapes.

pages.text: These animals have a different kind of life cycle. A life cycle is the series of changes an animal goes through during its life. Insects have fascinating life cycles. Some insects have a four-stage life cycle. The insect lives as an egg, larva (LAR- vuh), pupa (PYOO-puh), and an adult. Others have a three-stage life cycle. The insect is born as an egg, hatches as a nymph (NIMF), and changes into an adult.
pages.brief: Against a plain background, an egg, a larva, a pupa, and an adult are shown in a four-stage group. Beside them, an egg, a nymph, and an adult are shown in a three-stage group, showing two different insect life cycles.

pages.text: What Are Insects? There are more than 800,000 different kinds of insects. They include butterflies, beetles, fleas, and flies. Although they come in almost every shape, most insects have a few things in common.
pages.brief: A butterfly, a beetle, a flea, and a fly are shown together on a plain background. They are four of the more than 800,000 different kinds of insects, and most insects share a few things in common.

pages.text: All insects have six legs. Their bodies are divided into three parts. Most insects have wings and can fly. Most insects also wear their skeletons outside their bodies as hard shells. And all insects begin as eggs.
pages.brief: A single insect stands on a plain background, showing six legs, a body in three parts, wings, and a hard outer shell. Beside it, a small cluster of eggs shows that all insects begin as eggs.

pages.text: Egg You can find insect eggs everywhere, if you know where to look. Most insects lay their eggs near the food they like to eat. Moths and butterflies lay eggs underneath leaves. Dung beetles lay eggs in balls of animal poop. Many flies lay eggs on meat. Some insects even lay eggs on other animals.
pages.brief: Insect eggs are shown in several places: moth and butterfly eggs underneath a leaf, dung beetle eggs inside a ball of animal poop, fly eggs on meat, and eggs on another animal. The eggs sit near the food each kind of insect likes.

pages.text: Many insects make special cases to protect their eggs. One insect puts foam around its eggs. You may have seen this “cuckoo spit” in tall grass. Many insects lay eggs in pools, ponds, or streams. Others lay their eggs underground. Rarely, a female insect keeps the eggs inside her body. The eggs hatch, and the young are born alive.
pages.brief: In tall grass, a mass of eggs sits inside foam. Nearby, eggs are shown in a pool, a pond, and a stream, and other eggs are underground. A female insect is also shown with eggs hatching inside her body, with young born alive.

pages.text: Larva Most eggs hatch into a worm-like stage called a larva. Caterpillars, grubs, and maggots are larvae (LAR-vee). They have long bodies and many legs. Almost all larvae are eating machines. A larva can eat more than its own body weight in one day.
pages.brief: On a plain background, a caterpillar, a grub, and a maggot are shown as worm-like larvae with long bodies and many legs. One larva is eating a large piece of food, showing it can eat more than its own body weight in a day.

pages.text: Many larvae can destroy crops. Some larvae suck sap from crop roots. Others devour the leaves. Others eat fruits or vegetables. Beetle larvae can weaken and kill trees. Some moth larvae eat wool clothing. On the other hand, the silkworm, a moth larva, makes silk thread.
pages.brief: Larvae are shown on crop roots, sucking sap; on leaves, eating them; and on fruits and vegetables. Beetle larvae are shown weakening a tree, moth larvae are shown eating wool clothing, and a silkworm larva is shown making silk thread.

pages.text: Pupa Once the larva has grown, it must totally change its shape. And it must protect itself while it does so. Many larvae spin cocoons out of silk or grow hard shells. The pupa does not eat and does not move much. But inside, the insect is very busy changing shape. This change is called metamorphosis (MET-ah- MORF-oh-sis).
pages.brief: On a plain background, a larva is shown spinning a silk cocoon, and another pupa is shown inside a hard shell. The pupa sits still and does not eat, while inside its body is busy changing shape in metamorphosis.

pages.text: Adult After the metamorphosis is complete, the pupa hatches as an adult. The adult insect has wings, six legs, and three body parts. Many larvae that lived in water will hatch into adults that live on land. Larvae that lived underground will hatch above the soil. Adult insects will find mates, and the females will lay eggs. Sometimes, this is all the adults do. Mayfly adults live for only one day. Most other insects have longer adult lives. They eat, fly, hunt, and work.
pages.brief: An adult insect comes out of its pupa, with wings, six legs, and three body parts. A larva from water becomes an adult on land, and a larva from underground becomes an adult above the soil. Adults are shown finding mates, laying eggs, eating, flying, hunting, and working.

pages.text: Nymph In the three-stage life cycle, eggs do not hatch as larvae. They hatch as nymphs, which look like small adults. Some nymphs do not have full wings. Others, such as the dragonfly nymph, may live underwater.
pages.brief: In a three-stage life cycle, insect eggs hatch into nymphs that look like small adults. Some nymphs are shown with only partial wings. A dragonfly nymph is shown underwater, and other nymphs are shown as small adult-like insects.

pages.text: Nymphs do not turn into pupae. Instead, they shed their skin as they grow. Each time they shed their skin, they look more like an adult. Slowly, the nymph transforms into an adult.
pages.brief: On a plain background, a nymph is shown shedding its skin as it grows. After each shed, it looks more like an adult. The nymph slowly transforms into an adult, and no pupa stage is shown in this three-stage life cycle.

books.title: Big Machines
books.art_why: Big machines are real machines that exist today, so photographs fit best.

pages.text: Taking Resources from the Earth.11.
pages.brief: A cutaway view of the Earth shows resources buried deep inside, with a big machine ready to take them from the ground. The scene focuses on the Earth and the buried resources that big machines can remove.

pages.text: Introduction Work is done when something is moved from one place to another. Machines are used to do the work. They move things from one place to another. Some things are easy to move. Other things are not.
pages.brief: A machine moves a load from one place to another. One small, light-looking object sits nearby as an easy load, while a heavier object shows a harder load. The scene makes clear that machines do the work of moving things.

pages.text: Small machines are used for smaller jobs. Things like shovels are simple machines. They do not have many moving parts.
pages.brief: A shovel stands beside a small pile of dirt at a simple work site. The shovel looks simple, with few moving parts, ready for a smaller job. The scene focuses on the small machine and the load it can move.

pages.text: Big machines are used to move heavy things. They are used to build tall buildings. They are used to build roads and bridges. They are used to take resources from the earth.
pages.brief: Several big machines work around a tall building, a road and a bridge under construction, while another big machine takes resources from the earth. Heavy loads are being moved in each part of the scene.

pages.text: Building Tall Buildings It takes many big machines to build a tall building. Large power shovels called excavators dig deep holes in the ground. Some power shovels have huge buckets that can scoop a swimming pool-sized pile of dirt in one scoop. Others have clamlike buckets that take big bites out of the earth.
pages.brief: At a tall building site, large power shovels called excavators dig deep holes in the ground. One has a huge bucket scooping a swimming-pool-sized pile of dirt, while another has a clamlike bucket taking a big bite out of the earth.

pages.text: Do You Know? A bulldozer can move more dirt in fifteen minutes than a person can shovel in five days. Bulldozers are machines that move the dirt around. Giant dump trucks carry the dirt away. Concrete trucks carry concrete to the work site. Flatbed trucks carry steel beams and rods to the work site. Large cranes lift steel beams into place. They also carry buckets of concrete to workers high above ground.
pages.brief: At a busy work site, a bulldozer moves dirt while a giant dump truck carries dirt away. A concrete truck and a flatbed truck bring concrete, steel beams and rods. A large crane lifts steel beams and a bucket of concrete to workers high above the ground.

pages.text: Building Roads It takes many kinds of large machines to build a road. Large scrapers are used to get rid of trees and brush. They also are used to get rid of small hills. Loaders are used to dig up dirt and rocks. They put dirt and rocks into giant dump trucks that carry it away. Some dump trucks are so big that they can carry enough dirt to equal the weight of twenty elephants.
pages.brief: On a road-building site, a large scraper clears trees, brush and a small hill. A loader digs up dirt and rocks and puts them into a giant dump truck. The dump truck is so big it could carry a load equal to twenty elephants.

pages.text: Graders smooth out the roadway, and pavers lay the road surface onto the roadway. A roller following behind the paver presses down on the new road surface to make it smooth and flat.
pages.brief: On a road-building site, a grader smooths the roadway while a paver lays the new road surface behind it. A roller follows close behind the paver, pressing down on the fresh surface to make it smooth and flat.

pages.text: Taking Resources from the Earth There are many resources we need that are buried deep inside the Earth. We need big machines to get resources out. Oil drilling rigs are set up to remove oil.
pages.brief: A big oil drilling rig stands over ground where resources are buried deep inside the Earth. The rig is set up to remove oil, with its tall structure reaching upward above the drilling site.

pages.text: Large drills are used to get coal out of mines. Very large excavators dig up the earth in search of resources. Huge dump trucks then carry the resources to where they can be used to make products.
pages.brief: At a mine, a large drill works to get coal out of the ground. A very large excavator digs up the earth in search of resources, and a huge dump truck waits to carry the resources away to where they will be used to make products.

pages.text: Big Machines on Water There are big machines that move things on the water. Tugboats are machines that move other things over water by pulling and pushing. They pull barges. They push and pull large ships.
pages.brief: On the water, a tugboat pulls a barge behind it. Nearby, another tugboat pushes and pulls a large ship, showing how tugboats are big machines that move other things over water by pulling and pushing.

pages.text: Ocean liners are large ships that move people. Oil tankers are huge ships that carry massive amounts of oil. And container ships are stacked high with containers that carry things from place to place.
pages.brief: On the water, an ocean liner carries people while a huge oil tanker carries massive amounts of oil. A container ship is stacked high with containers that carry things from place to place across the sea.

pages.text: Big Machines in the Air Large airplanes carry people and cargo. A 747 is a giant passenger jet that can carry 400 to 450 people. The C-5 is a huge cargo plane. It is almost as long as a football field. Helicopters are flying machines too. The skycrane is a helicopter that is used to lift heavy objects. It can lift 15,000 pounds. It is used to carry things like bulldozers and power line towers into hard-to-reach places.
pages.brief: In the sky, a large passenger jet carries hundreds of people while a huge cargo plane flies nearby. A skycrane helicopter lifts a heavy object, carrying things like a bulldozer and a power line tower into a hard-to-reach place.

pages.text: Do You Know? Most big rigs have eighteen wheels or more. Can you imagine running over a bed of nails? That’s a lot of tires to change! You can see that many large machines are at work moving things from place to place. But probably the most common is the big rig. The big rig is made of two parts—the tractor and the trailer. Big rigs carry goods over roads that wind around the world.
pages.brief: On a road that winds into the distance, a big rig made of a tractor and a trailer carries goods. The trailer sits on many wheels, at least eighteen, and the big rig is shown as one of the most common large machines moving things from place to place.

books.title: Crocs and Gators
books.art_why: Keyword check says drawing, and the book mentions drawings of crocodilians.

pages.text: Never smile at a crocodile. That’s what the song from the movie Peter Pan says. After all, one bit off Captain Hook’s hand. Everyone thinks that crocodiles are fierce animals. And, in fact, they are. Crocodiles and alligators—like snakes, turtles, and lizards—are reptiles. They are members of a group of reptiles called crocodilians. Crocodilians have been on Earth since the age of dinosaurs. They even look a little like some of the dinosaurs from long ago.
pages.brief: A fierce crocodile with sharp teeth stands near a captain who has a hook for a hand, recalling the crocodile that bit him. Behind them, a large dinosaur stands, echoing the ancient age of dinosaurs and the crocodilian’s reptile relatives.

pages.text: Crocodilians spend time on land and in water. They use lungs to breathe. They have thick, scaly skin. Their body temperature does not stay the same like yours does. Instead, it changes with the temperature of the air and water around them. If it is too hot, these reptiles seek cool, shady places. Crocodilians live mostly in shallow water, swamps, and slow rivers. Most live in fresh water. But there are saltwater crocodiles, too. In fact, the saltwater crocodile may be the biggest reptile. Some reach lengths of over 7 meters (23 ft).
pages.brief: A huge saltwater crocodile stretches through shallow water beside a swampy riverbank, its thick, scaly skin and long body visible. On the bank, another crocodilian rests in a cool, shady spot. The scene shows crocodilians living both on land and in water.

pages.text: All crocodilians have short legs, and long bodies and tails. The four kinds of crocodilians have different kinds of jaws and teeth. All of them have sharp teeth. Let’s meet the different kinds of crocodilians. Alligators have short, broad snouts. Crocodiles have narrower snouts than alligators. They also have two large teeth that stick out. The drawings on this page show what alligators and crocodiles look like.
pages.brief: Two crocodilians stand side by side on the ground, their long bodies and tails stretching behind them. One has a short, broad snout like an alligator; the other has a narrower snout with two large teeth sticking out. Both show short legs and sharp teeth.

pages.text: Caimans live in Central and South America. The shape of their head is similar to that of a crocodile. Gharials are fish-eaters that live in India. They have long, narrow snouts. The drawings on this page show what caimans and gharials look like. Crocodilians are hard to see in water. Only the tops of their head and back show. They often look like a floating log. While they are swimming, their eyes and nostrils stick out of the water. They can still see and breathe when they are mostly underwater.
pages.brief: A caiman rests in Central America, its head shaped like a crocodile’s. A gharial in India opens its long, narrow snout to catch fish. Nearby, another crocodilian floats almost hidden in water, only the top of its head and back showing like a log, with eyes and nostrils above the surface.

pages.text: Crocodilians use large, powerful tails and webbed feet to move through water. When underwater, they close their ears and nostrils so that water stays out. They can also shut off their windpipe. This allows them to open their mouth without breathing in water. Crocodilians are fierce hunters. They use strong jaws to capture their prey. They eat animals as big as deer and cattle, and as small as fish and birds. They also will attack people. They cannot chew their food. They either swallow it whole or tear it apart. Sometimes they drag an animal underwater to drown it.
pages.brief: A crocodilian swims underwater with its powerful tail and webbed feet, ears and nostrils closed. Its jaws are wide open, showing it can open its mouth without breathing in water. At the water’s edge, a deer and a bird stand near, while fish swim nearby, showing the kinds of prey it hunts.

pages.text: Crocodilians are very fierce fighters. When a crocodilian attacks, it is almost impossible to escape. But they have their enemies, too. They may be killed in a fight with a leopard or lion. Some crocodilians lay their eggs in sand. Others make a nest with soil and plants. Newly hatched babies are mostly helpless. Many get eaten by other animals. The lucky ones have Mom to protect them after they hatch. Babies grow quickly. They are adults by the time they are 5 to 8 years old.
pages.brief: A mother crocodilian guards a nest of eggs in sand beside a mound of soil and plants. Several tiny hatchlings cluster near her, while a leopard and a lion watch from a distance. The babies look small and helpless, but the mother stays close, protecting the lucky ones as they begin to grow.

pages.text: Most crocodilians are endangered. In many parts of the world, people kill crocodilians for food and for their skins. Farmers destroy their homes to create land for growing crops and grazing animals. Crocodilians are also captured for use in wildlife parks. They are often killed when they grow too big. Around the world, people are helping to protect crocodilians. They put eggs in incubators to keep them safe. People then care for the babies until they grow strong enough to survive in the wild. Protecting them helps to keep nature in balance.
pages.brief: People place crocodilian eggs in an incubator to keep them safe. Nearby, people feed and care for small babies until they grow strong enough to survive in the wild. In the background, a farmer clears land and a hunter carries a skin, showing the dangers these reptiles face.

books.title: Ancient Egypt
books.art_why: Ancient Egypt predates photography, so the scenes must be drawn.

pages.text: Introduction Thousands of years ago, a group of people lived in the African country of Egypt. They lived on the banks of the Nile River. They were farmers and hunters. They used the river for boat travel. They were ruled by a king called a pharaoh.
pages.brief: Ancient Egyptian farmers and hunters work on the banks of the Nile River. A boat travels on the river. A king called a pharaoh is shown as the ruler of these people.

pages.text: Beliefs The ancient Egyptians believed that after someone died, he or she went to live in another world. They believed that a person’s next life would be like their present life. They thought the dead person would need the same tools and objects in their next life. So people were buried with many of the things that they owned.
pages.brief: Ancient Egyptians bury a dead person with many tools and objects they owned. They believe the person will live in another world and need the same things as in present life.

pages.text: Ancient Egyptians believed in a sun god. They believed that the king was related to this god. When the king died, he was given a very fancy burial. Many riches were buried with him. Queens were also given fancy burials.
pages.brief: Ancient Egyptians honor a sun god. A king is shown as related to this god. After the king dies, he receives a fancy burial with many riches. A queen also receives a fancy burial.

pages.text: After a king died, his body was preserved so that it would not rot. The king’s body was treated with spices, oils, and other things to preserve it. People believed that this would keep his spirit alive. The preserved body was called a mummy.
pages.brief: After a king dies, his body is treated with spices, oils, and other things so it will not rot. People believe this keeps his spirit alive. The preserved body is called a mummy.

pages.text: Pyramids The king was buried inside a huge stone structure called a pyramid. The pyramid was shaped to look like the Sun’s rays shining on Earth. People believed that the king would go to heaven on the rays of the Sun.
pages.brief: A huge stone pyramid stands on the land, shaped to look like the Sun's rays shining on Earth. The king is buried inside it. People believe the king will go to heaven on the Sun's rays.

pages.text: Pyramids took many years to build. When a king was still alive, people began building his pyramid. The stones used to make the pyramid were huge. It took hard work to get the stones out of the ground. It took harder work to move the stones to where the pyramid would be built. Some stones were moved on boats. Other stones were moved over land using big sleds.
pages.brief: People build a king's pyramid while he is still alive. Workers struggle to get huge stones out of the ground and move them to the building place. Some stones travel on boats; other stones are moved over land on big sleds.

pages.text: Inside the pyramid was a tomb. This was a special room where the king’s body was placed. Many objects were put in the tomb. There were statues, paintings, and many gold things.
pages.brief: Inside the pyramid is a tomb, a special room where the king's body is placed. Many objects are put in the tomb with him: statues, paintings, and many gold things.

pages.text: Many hidden tunnels and rooms were built inside a pyramid. They were built to trick anyone who tried to steal things from the tomb. Giant stones were put in front of the doorway of the real tomb. They were used to keep out thieves. Still, almost every king’s tomb has been robbed over the years. But the pyramids still stand.
pages.brief: Hidden tunnels and rooms are built inside a pyramid to trick anyone trying to steal from the tomb. Giant stones stand in front of the real tomb's doorway to keep out thieves. The pyramids still stand even though almost every king's tomb has been robbed.

pages.text: The Great Pyramid at Giza is a famous pyramid. It was built for King Khufu. It has more than two million blocks of stone. Other pyramids near it were built for the king’s relatives. A statue called the Sphinx guards all of the pyramids. The Sphinx has the face of a king and the body of a lion.
pages.brief: The Great Pyramid at Giza, built for King Khufu, has more than two million blocks of stone. Other pyramids near it were built for the king's relatives. A statue called the Sphinx, with a king's face and a lion's body, guards all the pyramids.

pages.text: Conclusion Studying the ancient Egyptians teaches us a lot about life long ago. We can learn about the tools these people used and clothes they wore. We can learn about the food they ate and the gods they worshipped. By studying ancient Egyptians, we know that they had a great culture.
pages.brief: A group of people study the ancient Egyptians to learn about life long ago. The scene shows their tools, the clothes they wore, the food they ate, and the gods they worshipped. By studying ancient Egyptians, we know that they had a great culture.

books.title: Fantastic Flying Machines
books.art_why: It covers early flight history and inventions where real photos of the events are impossible.

pages.text: Introduction Imagine if you could fly like a bird. Where would you go? What would you see? Today, many people can fly thanks to fantastic flying machines.
pages.brief: A bird soars high above the open sky beside several different flying machines, showing that many people can fly today. Below, a wide world stretches out with distant places to go and things to see.

pages.text: People have always wanted to fly. They watched birds fly, and some tried tying wings to their arms. Long ago, an artist even drew plans to make a helicopter. He drew his idea, but he didn’t build it. History of Flight People kept trying to fly. Two French brothers made the first hot-air balloon. Another man made the first glider that worked. Later, someone made a better glider that could sail in the air for a long time.
pages.brief: Historical flight scene: a man with tied-on wings watches birds; an artist sketches a helicopter design; two French brothers stand by a hot-air balloon; a man pilots an early glider; a later glider sails in the air.

pages.text: Brothers named Orville and Wilbur Wright studied all these ideas. They thought about how some ideas worked and why some didn’t work. They tested their own ideas. Finally, they designed an airplane that worked. One day, Orville flew the plane for one full minute. It flew for 260 meters (850 ft.). People could fly! Airplanes Airplanes have changed a lot since the early days of flight. Today’s large airplanes carry about 450 people on trips. They also carry people’s bags and cargo. Has your family flown on one?
pages.brief: Orville Wright flies a working airplane low over open ground for one full minute, covering 260 meters; in another part of the scene, a large modern airplane carries about 450 people with their bags and cargo.

pages.text: Many modern planes that are built to fly high or fast use jet engines. A jet engine forces hot gases in a stream behind it. That force pushes a plane forward. Many planes have propeller engines. Propeller blades spin like a fan’s blades.
pages.brief: A high, fast modern plane flies in the sky with a jet engine blasting a stream of hot gas behind it, pushing the plane forward. Beside it, a propeller plane shows fan-like blades spinning like a fan.

pages.text: Planes carry things quickly over long distances. Cargo planes and mail planes fly around the world. Big military planes carry trucks, food, and troops. Helicopters Helicopters can land almost anywhere. They can also fly backward and sideways. They can even stop in midair!
pages.brief: A cargo plane and a mail plane fly over the world carrying loads. A big military plane carries trucks, food and troops. Nearby, a helicopter stops in midair, flies backward and sideways, and lands on a small spot.

pages.text: Some helicopters are designed to lift heavy loads. These helicopters need two rotors on top. Firefighters sometimes use these types of helicopters to fight forest fires. Helicopters are much faster than cars. They can be used as ambulances. Police use them to watch neighborhoods from the sky. Helicopters help rescue people who are lost, too.
pages.brief: A heavy-lift helicopter with two rotors on top lifts a heavy load. The same type of helicopter helps firefighters fight a forest fire below. Another helicopter acts as an ambulance, a police helicopter watches a neighborhood from the sky, and one rescues lost people.

pages.text: Many people watch the beautiful hot-air balloons dot the sky. Blimps and Balloons Hot-air balloons are pushed by the wind. They fly slowly and are very quiet. Many balloons have fun and colorful designs. Most blimps have two small propeller engines. Pilots steer them where they want to go. Some blimps are used to take photos of sporting events.
pages.brief: People on the ground watch colorful hot-air balloons dot the sky, drifting slowly and quietly with the wind. Nearby, a blimp with two small propeller engines is steered by a pilot and takes photos of a sporting event below.

pages.text: Rockets and Spaceships Powerful rockets work like big engines. Rocket engines force hot air and gas out the back to create thrust. Rockets helped people fly to the Moon and back. A space shuttle rides a rocket into space. When it comes back to Earth, its wings let it land like an airplane.
pages.brief: A powerful rocket launches upward, forcing hot air and gas out the back to create thrust. It carries people toward the Moon and back. A space shuttle rides a rocket into space, then returns to Earth with wings and lands like an airplane.

pages.text: Other Ways to Fly Once, people only dreamed of flying like birds. Now, hang gliders drift on air. You can ride in a hot- air balloon. Airplanes fly everywhere. Where would you like to fly? Wright, Orville and Wilbur, 7 space shuttle, 18 Index jet engines.
pages.brief: A hang glider drifts on the air, a person rides in a hot-air balloon, and airplanes fly across the sky. The scene shows many ways people can fly now, after once only dreaming of flying like birds.

books.title: Sign Language
books.art_why: Real-world topic about living people and communication, not a single named famous person.

pages.text: Sign Language Ff Gg Ee Dd Cc Bb Aa Mm Ll Kk Jj Ii Hh Ss Rr Qq Pp Oo Nn Yy Xx Zz Ww Vv Uu Tt.
pages.brief: A series of close-up photographs shows hands and fingers forming each letter of the alphabet in sign language. The hand shapes are presented one after another, simple and clear, filling the frame against a plain background.

pages.text: Introduction Sign language is a way that deaf people communicate. It uses the hands, fingers, face, and body. People can spell letters and make words in sign language. Just like there are many words in spoken languages, sign languages also have many words.
pages.brief: Two deaf adults face each other in a bright room, communicating with hands, fingers, facial expressions, and body posture. One signs a letter, then a whole word, while the other watches closely. Their hands and faces fill the scene.

pages.text: People who are deaf or hard of hearing use their hands to make letters and words. This is called sign language. Thomas Gallaudet (ga-luh-DET) helped start a school for deaf students in the United States in 1817. The school used French Sign Language, Native American Sign Language, and other hand signs to create American Sign Language (ASL).
pages.brief: A schoolroom for deaf students in the United States in 1817. Thomas Gallaudet stands with a teacher and students who make hand signs for letters and words. The students use French Sign Language, Native American Sign Language, and other hand signs together.

pages.text: Learning Sign Language Today, sign language is taught to deaf people when they are very young. When a deaf child is playing with a ball, an adult uses two hands to make a sign for ball. Then, the adult points to the ball. The sign for ball is called a whole word sign. Deaf children also learn to use their fingers to make letters. They learn each letter of the alphabet. Making these different types of signs is called signing.
pages.brief: A deaf child plays with a ball while an adult kneels beside them. The adult makes the whole-word sign for ball with two hands, then points to the ball. In another moment, the child practices finger shapes for alphabet letters.

pages.text: Aa Bb Cc.
pages.brief: Close-up photographs show three hand shapes for the letters A, B, and C in sign language. Each hand is shown clearly against a plain background, with fingers positioned differently for each letter. The three views are simple and centered, helping a viewer see how the hand changes from one letter to the next.

pages.text: Some signs tell what a person needs. For example, food or drink. Babies sometimes learn signs for their needs, too. Baby signs are different from sign language. Babies can learn to make a fist when they want milk. They can learn to shape their hands like a cup and pretend to drink when they are thirsty.
pages.brief: A baby reaches toward a caregiver and makes a fist to ask for milk. The caregiver shapes a hand like a cup and pretends to drink to show thirst. On a table nearby, a cup and a small snack show food and drink needs.

pages.text: Many Kinds of Sign Language There are many kinds of spoken language. The same is true for sign language! Sign languages can be different from country to country. They can also be different from group to group in the same country.
pages.brief: People from different countries and communities stand in small groups, each using different hand signs. One group signs in one style, another group signs in another style, and a third group uses still different signs. They are all communicating with hands and faces.

pages.text: Many people in the United States and Canada use ASL. Some deaf Black Americans use a kind of ASL called Black American Sign Language. Members of the Native Plains groups in the United States created Plains Indian Sign Language. The signs can be different, but they are all used to communicate!
pages.brief: In the United States and Canada, people use ASL. Some deaf Black Americans use Black American Sign Language. Members of Native Plains groups use Plains Indian Sign Language. Photographs show signers from these communities making different hand signs, all communicating.

pages.text: Famous Sign Language Users Helen Keller Helen Keller was blind and deaf. She used her sense of touch to communicate. People used their fingers to sign letters on the palm of her hand. She touched people’s lips as they spoke. She understood what they were saying by the changing shape of their lips. Keller was very smart. She went to college and wrote six books.
pages.brief: Helen Keller, blind and deaf, sits with a teacher. The teacher signs letters into the palm of her hand with fingers. Helen touches the teacher's lips as the teacher speaks, feeling the changing lip shapes. Books and a college setting suggest her education and writing.

pages.text: Heather Whitestone In 1994, Heather Whitestone became Miss America. She was the first deaf person to win the contest. She danced to music she couldn’t hear. Since winning the crown, Heather has spoken and written books about living as a deaf person.
pages.brief: Heather Whitestone stands on a stage in a Miss America contest, wearing a crown and dancing to music. She is the first deaf person to win the contest. Later, she speaks to an audience and writes books about living as a deaf person.

pages.text: Blanche Wilkins Williams Blanche Wilkins Williams was born in 1876. She became deaf as a child. She was a good student. Williams became a teacher for Black deaf and blind children. She also cared about equality for Black deaf people. She helped Black deaf people become leaders.
pages.brief: Blanche Wilkins Williams, born in 1876, stands in a classroom as a teacher for Black deaf and blind children. She works with students who use hand signs. In another scene, she speaks with Black deaf adults and helps them become leaders.

pages.text: Conclusion Deaf people use sign language to communicate. There are many kinds of sign languages, just like there are many kinds of languages that people speak. If you want to learn a new language, try sign language!
pages.brief: Deaf people of different ages communicate with sign language in everyday places: a classroom, a playground, and a community center. Hands, faces, and bodies make many kinds of signs. A child watches and tries a new sign, showing that sign language is a language anyone can learn.

books.title: Introducing Planet Earth
books.art_why: The keyword check points to drawing for this personified Earth book.

pages.text: Let me introduce myself. I am Planet Earth. I am the luckiest planet in our solar system. I can support life!
pages.brief: A round, blue-and-green illustrated Earth floats in starry space, shown as a friendly character introducing itself. Oceans and land are visible on its surface. A warm glow surrounds the planet, suggesting it is lively and able to support life.

pages.text: Look at Mercury so close to the Sun. Hot, hot, hot. Even one of my desert rats could not live in that heat! Cold dwarf planet Pluto sits so far from the Sun. Brrrr. How would you like to be a frozen Popsicle planet? Not me.
pages.brief: Mercury sits close to a blazing Sun, glowing with intense heat. Far across dark space, tiny Pluto is icy and frozen. A small desert rat on Earth looks toward the scorching scene, showing that even a heat-loving animal could not live on Mercury.

pages.text: I have all the things life needs— land, water, air, and energy from the Sun. I have five oceans and seven huge pieces of land called continents. On land, I even have lakes and rivers filled with fresh water that plants and animals need.
pages.brief: A wide view of illustrated Earth shows blue oceans, seven large landmasses, and wispy air around the planet. Sunlight streams down. On land, lakes and rivers hold fresh water, with green plants and animals nearby.

pages.text: I spin like a top so that all living things have day and night. People call this rotating.
pages.brief: Illustrated Earth spins like a top in space. One side faces the bright Sun and is lit for daytime, while the opposite side is dark for nighttime. Curved lines suggest the turning motion around the planet.

pages.text: Try This! Want to see what makes day and night? Get a flashlight and a friend to be the Sun. You be Earth. Earth spins around slowly. It’s daytime on the side of your body facing the Sun! It’s nighttime on the side turned away from the Sun.
pages.brief: A child stands as Earth while a friend holds a flashlight like the Sun. The child turns slowly. The side of the child facing the flashlight is bright, showing daytime; the side turned away is shadowed, showing nighttime.

pages.text: Because I am round like a ball, sunlight hits me unevenly. This makes parts of me hot and parts of me cold. My belly gets the most direct sunlight, so it is hottest along my belt. This area is called the equator.
pages.brief: A round illustrated Earth floats in sunlight. Bright rays strike the planet unevenly. The middle belt around Earth’s belly receives the most direct sunlight and glows warm, while the top and bottom are less bright. This middle area is the hot equator.

pages.text: My North and South Poles get the least direct sunlight. The Sun’s rays are weaker here than at my equator. These areas are my coldest. Whether it’s hot, cold, or in between, creatures live all over me.
pages.brief: Illustrated Earth shows weak sunlight reaching the North and South Poles, leaving both ends cold and pale. Between the icy poles, forests, deserts, oceans, and other habitats hold many creatures living in hot, cold, and mild places.

pages.text: People live on all my continents; a few even live around the South Pole in Antarctica. Most people live in my milder parts where they can build homes and grow crops.
pages.brief: People appear on every illustrated continent, including a small group in snowy Antarctica near the South Pole. Most people gather in milder regions, where they build homes and grow crops in fields under a bright sky.

pages.text: People travel all over my planet. Long ago, people got lost when sailing across my oceans. They needed a way to identify locations. So they invented a global grid, or lines that cross each other to form points anywhere on Earth. The lines that run north and south are longitude lines. The lines running east and west are latitude lines. This grid tells people where they are.
pages.brief: A sailing ship crosses a wide illustrated ocean. Above the scene, a globe shows crossing lines that form a global grid: lines running north and south and lines running east and west, meeting at points across Earth.

pages.text: Oh, I almost forgot. I am tilted, too. As I travel around the Sun during my yearlong trip, I stay in my tilt. Sometimes I tilt toward the Sun, and sometimes away from it. My tilt creates seasons. In January, my top half, or northern half, is tilted away from the Sun. That’s winter when children in the northern half go sledding. At the same time, the southern half is pointed toward the Sun. It’s summer there.
pages.brief: A tilted illustrated Earth travels around the Sun. In January, Earth’s northern half leans away from the Sun, showing winter with children sledding on snow. The southern half leans toward the Sun, showing warm summer there.

pages.text: When I get halfway around the Sun and it’s July, I’m still tilted. But this time, my northern half is tilted toward the Sun, and it’s summer. My southern half is pointed away from the Sun, and it’s winter there. I am a fair planet. I give each of my halves seasons and equal amounts of sunlight. They just get it at different times of year.
pages.brief: In July, the same tilted Earth is halfway around the Sun. Its northern half now leans toward the Sun, bringing summer, while the southern half leans away and has winter. Both halves receive seasons and equal sunlight at different times of year.

pages.text: To all life on Earth, I make you a promise. I will rotate every 24 hours to give you daytime and nighttime. I will continue to tilt to give you seasons. I will travel around the Sun once each year. And I will do all these things for billions of years to come.
pages.brief: Illustrated Earth glows in space with a calm, promising expression. Around it, small scenes show the planet turning for day and night, tilting through seasons, and traveling once around the Sun each year, continuing for billions of years.

pages.text: I am a planet you can trust.
pages.brief: A friendly illustrated Earth stands alone in space, looking steady and dependable. Its blue oceans and green land are clear, and a soft glow surrounds the planet, matching the calm promise that Earth can be trusted.

books.title: World Holidays
books.art_why: World holidays are real cultural celebrations people observe today.

pages.text: Introduction Introduction Introduction People all over the world celebrate holidays that are full of traditions. Traditions are the special ways people do something. People celebrate holidays by preparing and eating food, playing games, singing songs, and telling stories.
pages.brief: In homes around the world, diverse families and children prepare and eat food, play games, sing songs, and tell stories together. Some children help serve food, some play a game, and others sing or listen to a story, showing holiday traditions shared by people across the world.

pages.text: Chinese New Year Chinese New Year Chinese New Year Many people celebrate Chinese New Year. People celebrate the arrival of spring and wish for good luck. They put good luck sayings in their homes and watch a colorful Lion Dance. It uses loud noises to chase away bad luck. People also give gifts to others.
pages.brief: In a home, people place good luck sayings for Chinese New Year and welcome the arrival of spring. At a Lion Dance, people watch the colorful dance use loud noises to chase away bad luck. People also exchange gifts with one another.

pages.text: Where Started: Europe Christmas Christmas Christmas Christmas can be celebrated at different times, but many people celebrate on December 25th. Christmas usually lasts only a day, but the celebration may last longer. Many people place a tree in their homes. They decorate the tree with colorful lights. People sing songs and give gifts to family and friends. They also share toys, clothes, and food with others who need them.
pages.brief: On December 25th, in a home decorated for Christmas, a tree shines with colorful lights. Family and friends sing songs and exchange gifts. People also gather toys, clothes, and food to share with others who need them, showing the holiday's giving spirit.

pages.text: Hanukkah Hanukkah Hanukkah Other people celebrate Hanukkah. Hanukkah lasts eight nights. People light a candle each night in a holder called a menorah. During Hanukkah, people sing songs and eat with family and friends. They get small gifts and money to share with others. People also play a game with a top called a dreidel.
pages.brief: At home during Hanukkah, a family lights one candle in a menorah for each of the eight nights. They sing songs, eat together, and share small gifts and money. People play a game with a dreidel top.

pages.text: Holi Holi Holi Some people celebrate Holi. During Holi, people celebrate the end of winter and the arrival of spring. People sing and dance. They decorate with lots of colors and wear colorful clothes. They even spray family and friends with colorful powders and water. It is a time of joy and fun.
pages.brief: During Holi, family and friends celebrate the end of winter and the arrival of spring. People wear colorful clothes, sing, dance, and spray one another with colorful powders and water in a joyful, fun time.

pages.text: Kwanzaa Kwanzaa Kwanzaa Other people celebrate Kwanzaa. It is an important time of the year for friends and family. Kwanzaa lasts for seven days. Each night, people light candles in a holder called a kinara. There are seven candles in the kinara, one for each night of Kwanzaa.
pages.brief: For Kwanzaa, a family gathers at home for seven days. Each night they light candles in a kinara. The kinara holds seven candles, one for each night of Kwanzaa, as friends and family share this important time.

pages.text: During Kwanzaa, people celebrate by eating together and giving gifts. An mkeka, or mat, with vegetables is put in the home. Special items are placed on this mat. People tell traditional stories with family and friends.
pages.brief: During Kwanzaa, family and friends eat together and give gifts. In the home, an mkeka mat holds vegetables and special items. People tell traditional stories together around it, sharing this important time of the year.

pages.text: Where Started: Middle East New Year New Year New Year People all over the world celebrate the New Year. People use different calendars to tell when a new year starts. They have many traditions. Many people celebrate with fireworks and songs. They may toss colorful pieces of paper in the air. People also might wish each other good luck for the new year.
pages.brief: People all over the world celebrate New Year with fireworks and songs. Some toss colorful pieces of paper into the air. Friends and family wish one another good luck, using different calendars to tell when the new year starts.

pages.text: Where Started: Middle East Ramadan Ramadan Ramadan Other people celebrate Ramadan. It lasts one month. During Ramadan, many people eat only before the sun comes up, and after it goes down. People show their thanks for the things they have. It is a time to think about other people and do nice things for them.
pages.brief: During Ramadan, which lasts one month, people eat before the sun comes up and after it goes down. They give thanks for what they have, think about other people, and do nice things for them.

pages.text: Conclusion Conclusion Conclusion Holidays are often a special time for people. Many holidays are celebrated all over the world. People celebrate the holidays in some ways that are different, and some ways that are the same.
pages.brief: Holidays are often a special time for people around the world. Diverse families and friends celebrate in ways that are different and in ways that are the same, coming together in a shared holiday feeling.

pages.text: A Celebration Timetable A Celebration Timetable A Celebration Timetable Holidays occur all year long. Here are some holidays and when they are celebrated. Chinese New Year • Chinese New Year is based on the Chinese calendar. • It is celebrated in late January or early February. It lasts for 15 days. Christmas • Christmas is celebrated on December 25th or January 6th each year. • It lasts one day. However, people often celebrate this holiday over many days. Do You Know? Many people around the world follow the Gregorian calendar, often referred to as the Western calendar. This calendar measures approximately 365 days in each year. Hanukkah • Hanukkah is based on the Jewish calendar. • It begins in middle or late December and lasts eight nights.
pages.brief: People look at calendars to see when holidays happen through the year. Chinese New Year comes in late January or early February and lasts fifteen days. Christmas is on December 25th or January 6th. Hanukkah begins in middle or late December and lasts eight nights.

pages.text: Holi • Holi lasts 15 days and is celebrated each March on the day after the full moon. Kwanzaa • Kwanzaa begins on December 26th and ends on January 1st. It lasts seven days. New Year • Many people celebrate the coming of the new year on the night before New Year’s Day. • New Year’s Day is January 1st or the beginning of spring. Ramadan • Ramadan is based on the Muslim calendar. The calendar is 354 days long. • Celebrating Ramadan lasts about 29 or 30 days. Math Minute • How many days is the Muslim calendar shorter than the Western calendar? • How many days do Chinese New Year and Kwanzaa last altogether?
pages.brief: A calendar display shows days for holidays through the year. Holi lasts fifteen days each March. Kwanzaa begins December 26th and ends January 1st. New Year's Day is January 1st or the beginning of spring. Ramadan lasts about twenty-nine or thirty days.

books.title: Shoes Around the World
books.art_why: Shoes, places and people shown all exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Shoes Around the World.
pages.brief: A bright row of shoes from around the world laid out on a clean, light background: soft Moroccan slippers, wooden Dutch clogs, tall wooden Japanese geta, upturned Lapland boots, pointed cowboy boots and thick-soled African sandals, all photographed close up and evenly lit.

pages.text: Howdie from Australia Hello from Holland Introduction I love shoes—all kinds of shoes. My grandma loves to travel. Last year, she took a trip around the world. She sent my brother postcards from all the places she visited. Grandma sent me shoes!
pages.brief: A young child sits on the floor holding a pair of shoes, grinning, with more shoes and postcards spread around her. A postcard showing a sunny beach and another showing windmills rest beside a small suitcase, and a brother looks over her shoulder.

pages.text: Babouches First, Grandma sent me some babouches (bah-BOO-shes) from Morocco. They are soft and comfortable like slippers. But you can wear them outdoors. Grandma says they are made of camel hair. They are easy to slip on and off.
pages.brief: A pair of soft Moroccan babouches in warm yellow leather rests on a patterned tile floor, and a child's hand slips one on easily. The slippers look soft and comfortable, with no laces or buckles, ready to be worn outdoors in a sunny courtyard.

pages.text: Klompen Next, Grandma sent me some klompen (KLOM-pen) from Holland. They make a clip-clop sound when I walk. That’s because klompen are made of wood.
pages.brief: A pair of pale wooden klompen clogs stands on a brick path outside a Dutch house, and a child walks past wearing them, one foot lifted mid-step. The thick carved wood is clearly visible, along with tulips and a canal in the background.

pages.text: People used to wear klompen as work shoes on farms and in factories and mines.
pages.brief: A farmer wearing wooden klompen squelches across a muddy farmyard beside a cow, while behind him a factory building and a mine entrance stand in the distance, showing the farms, factories and mines where people once wore wooden work shoes.

pages.text: Geta In geta (GEH-tah) sandals, I can be much taller! Grandma sent these tall wooden geta from Japan. Both men and women used to wear these sandals with their beautiful silk kimonos (ki-MOH-nohz). The high wooden platforms kept their kimonos out of the dust and mud.
pages.brief: A woman in a flowing silk kimono walks on tall wooden geta sandals along a dusty path, holding her hem clear of the mud. Beside her a man in a kimono and geta steps carefully, the high wooden platforms lifting both of them above the dirt.

pages.text: People started wearing wooden geta over 2,000 years ago. Today, Grandma says this traditional shoe is usually worn only at ceremonies and other special times. In Japan, Grandma learned how to walk in geta. You have to slide your foot back so your heel hangs off the edge a little. Then you pinch your toes together around the strap with each step.
pages.brief: Close-up of feet in wooden geta on a stone path, heels hanging just off the back edge of the platforms and toes gripping the strap. Behind, people in kimonos walk in geta at a special ceremony outside a Japanese shrine.

pages.text: Sámi Reindeer Boots Next, Grandma sent me some Sámi (SAH-mee) reindeer boots from Lapland. That’s the part of Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Russia that is north of the Arctic Circle. These boots are very warm.
pages.brief: A pair of Sámi reindeer boots with curled toes and fur trim stands in deep snow in Lapland, north of the Arctic Circle. A Sámi person in a thick winter coat holds one boot up, snowy pine trees and low winter light behind.

pages.text: See how the toes turn up? That’s to help people walk through the snow. The Sámi are the Native people of the Lapland region. Their reindeer boots helped develop the first ski boots. The boots tie around your ankle to keep the snow out and the heat in.
pages.brief: A Sámi person in a fur-trimmed coat strides through deep snow wearing reindeer boots with upturned toes, the laces tied snugly around the ankle. The curved toes ride up over the snow, and old wooden ski boots lie nearby for comparison.

pages.text: Cowboy Boots Near the end of her trip, Grandma went to Australia. My cowboy boots came from there. Did you know cowboy boots are pointed at the toes? That is so cowboys and cowgirls can easily slip their feet into saddle stirrups.
pages.brief: A pair of pointed cowboy boots stands in the dust beside a saddle, the narrow toes lined up with the metal stirrups. An Australian paddock with eucalyptus trees and a fence stretches out behind under a wide blue sky.

pages.text: Cowboy boots are tall to protect you from cactuses and snakes. I hope Grandma did not run into any snakes in Australia!
pages.brief: A cowgirl in tall leather cowboy boots walks through dry scrubland, a spiky cactus beside her and a snake slithering across the red dirt ahead. The high boot tops cover her legs for protection from thorns and bites.

pages.text: Hausa Sandals Last, Grandma sent me some sandals from Nigeria made by the Hausa people. It’s very hot there. That’s why these sandals have such thick soles. Thick soles protect your feet from the hot ground. Also, sandals let air move around your feet to keep you cool.
pages.brief: A pair of Hausa sandals with thick leather soles rests on hot sandy ground in Nigeria, and a person's bare feet stand in them, straps across the toes. The open design lets air move around the feet in the strong sunlight.

pages.text: Conclusion People around the world wear different kinds of shoes. They wear different shoes at different times. They wear different shoes for different reasons. Just like me!
pages.brief: Children from around the world stand in a row on a plain background, each wearing different shoes — wooden clogs, soft slippers, tall geta, cowboy boots and thick sandals — smiling at the camera, their different footwear lined up side by side.
